Question: If given a choice, what would you like to have? Money or power?
Answer: I prepared for the civil services examination at IIT Delhi, which used to be UPSC's garh (centre) those days (around 1990). The toppers of GATE from Northern India used to get admission to IIT Delhi in whichever branch they could get into, and then they used to prepare for CSE while doing their M-Tech. One of the most prospective IAS was my hostel neighbour Satyendra Gupta (SG), who was the all-India topper of GATE on Mechanical Engineering and a Gold Medalist in IIT Roorkee. He, like us, joined IIT Delhi to prepare for IAS. However, after a couple of weeks, when I visited his hostel room, I saw no UPSC books on his table. On being asked, he told me that he dropped the idea of writing UPSC, “I will do M Tech and attempt getting 10 point grades. Then I will do PhD from the US and become a professor.” When I tried to persuade him to write UPSC, he asked, “Why do you want to go for UPSC?” I parroted the standard reply, “Because, as a civil servant, you enjoy great power and the best perks like vehicles and big government houses.” He replied back, ‘I disagree. Power is a great responsibility and you can’t enjoy it unless you misuse it. As an IPS officer, you have to work round the clock, fight criminals and hardly get proper sleep at night. As an IAS officer, you deal with filthy politicians, corrupt contractors and officers within the department. If you take action, you make enemies and if you don’t use power, you lose all respect. Similarly, there is no fun in having a government vehicle, which is only for the official purpose, unless you misuse them for personal use.’ I did not agree with his views then and chose to become a civil servant, while Satyendra chose his path and is now a professor at the University of Southern California. However, after working for more than 25 years as an IRS officer, I now agree with him. Power is not a privilege, but a great responsibility. Whenever you exercise your power against anyone, you make them your personal enemies and you are hated for it. However, if you fail to exercise your power you are still hated for being incompetent and useless. For instance, most people hate Modi because he exercises his power to the fullest. People also hated Dr Manmohan Singh because he did not exercise his powers. Most people seek power because they can (mis)use power to make money, intimidate their rivals or become popular. When such people are caught, or voted out by people, they lose their power, money and prestige in society. On the other side, money can provide you lasting happiness and peace of mind, if earned through legal and moral means. While you can lose power anytime (You may be a PM/CM/DM today and a nobody tomorrow), money is more secure, if invested properly. Power is, therefore, desired mostly by poor and middle-class people, who want to feel important in the eyes of society and secretly believe that they can make lots of illegal money through corruption. However, if you are rich, you rarely seek power, as money itself is a power besides being a means to enjoy your life. You might have seen the children of many top politicians and civil servants starting a company or joining top companies to make lots of money. However, you would rarely find the children of top businessmen writing civil services examinations or joining politics to acquire power. When I understood the folly of power, I left the IRS when I had 11+ years of job left. Hence, If I am given a choice, I will choose money (lawfully earned) over power any day. I am not aware of any country in the world whose citizens are so respected and welcomed in the most developed nations. Question: How did growing up in poverty in India affect you personally?
Answer: When I look back at my childhood, I feel that I grew up in poverty. However, we did not feel poor back then because our other relatives were even poorer. After all, we lived in Lucknow, had 24x7 electricity, and received an education in government or missionary schools, a luxury for our relatives in the village. Many of my friends came from well-off families who lived much better quality of life. However, I never felt envious of them. Instead, I took it as a challenge to perform better than them despite our poverty and used poverty as a motivation rather than a handicap. Growing up in relative poverty affected me in multiple ways. I have also learned that poverty is romantic only in fiction and a curse in the real world. Unlike many people, I don’t have sweet childhood memories. I rarely think about childhood, as it always leaves a bitter taste in my mouth. If I had been born into a more affluent family, perhaps I would have enjoyed my childhood better and even achieved greater success in life. However, my humble childhood has taught me many valuable lessons in life at an early age, which I would have completely missed if I had been born into a rich family. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: Why are we so poor and others are rich?
Answer: In the modern world, the value of everything is determined not by its inherent quality or importance but by demand and supply. For instance, there can be nothing more valuable for a human being than food, water and air. However, in the world, food is more valuable than water, which is more valuable than air because On the other hand, we find that gold is costly. At the cost of one kg of gold, you can buy a lifetime supply of food. This is not because gold is more important than food but because the supply of gold is very limited while its demand is millions of times greater. Diamonds are even more costly because their supply is meagre, but their demand is very high. Like material things such as food, water, air, gold, and diamonds, individuals' value also depends on the demand for their skills compared to the supply of the skill in the market. For instance, labourers require little skill to do their job, and any healthy person can do this job. As a result, developing countries have a vast labour force supply compared to demand. Their value is the lowest, and their people are the poorest. On the other side, you have to spend years in schools and collages to acquire the knowledge and develop the skill of a software developer or manager. In many developed countries, however, most people have a higher level of education, and fewer people are available to work as manual labourers. Hence, the demand for manual labourers is greater than the supply. As a result, labourers in developed countries are much better paid than their counterparts in poorer countries and even better than their educated counterparts in their own country. Anyone can make huge money and become rich if they acquire a skill that is in high demand, but its supply is less. For instance, the highest international and domestic packages offered during IIT Bombay placements in 2023 were INR 3.67 crore per annum and INR 1.68 crore per annum, respectively, while the average package offered was INR 21.82 LPA.[1] Therefore, if you acquire education from a top college and the top level skill, you can earn more than 100 times more income than the graduates of ordinary college and more than 200 times more than unskilled workers. Even within the same college, the most skilled person would earn 10 times more than the lowest classmate. If you are poor, it is because you (or your forefathers) have not acquired a high-demand-low-supplu skill. If some people are rich, it is because they, their parents, or their grandparents have acquired the high-demand, low-supply skills that enhance their value in the market. If you wish to become wealthy, you must invest your time, money and effort in developing difficult-to-acquire but much-sought-after skills to command a better income in the market. Once you become wealthy, not only will you become rich, but your future generations will also enjoy the fruit of your labour and live better lives. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: What motivates India's richest man to continue working hard while others have retired? Is it solely due to work culture or are there other factors at play?
Answer: When I was in government service, there used to be a retirement farewell function on the last day of almost every month in honour of the retiree employee. In one place, a superintendent used to conduct most of the retirement functions. He would typically start his speech with the following words, “In the life of government servants, two things are certain. One is death, and the other is the retirement. While only God knows when a person would die, the retirement date is known to everyone when the government officer joins the service.” In India, government officers typically retire (superannuation) on the last day of the month in which they complete 60 years. Likewise, there is a retirement date for the corporate sector as well. It is important to understand that working people don’t retire voluntarily; they are forced to do so at the retirement age. Most people in modern times are so fit physically and mentally at the age of 60 that they are considered capable of leading the entire department of the state or central government or their organisation. For instance, the IPS Prashant Kumar is in his 60th year. He is the DGP of Uttar Pradesh, heading the police force of hundreds of thousands of police personnel in the biggest state of India. However, next year, he will retire and become a nobody on the day he crosses 60 years. [1] How come the most able person becomes disabled within one day? Most people can work quite efficiently in the 60s and 70s and would not like to retire if they had the option. For instance, in the USA, there is no retirement age for Supreme Court judges, and people continue to work as judges of the Apex Court even in their 80s. Justice John Paul Stevens performed the function as a Supreme Court Judge even when he was over 90 years old.[2] It is also common to see old politicians in their 70s and 80s occupying the top government positions as the head of the nation and leading their nation. The current Prime Minister of India is 74 years old, while the President of the United States is more than 81 years old. Most people would like to work as long as they can. If you are an entrepreneur, you can work as long as you want. Hence, most of the wealthiest people in the world never retire from work till late age. However, if you are an employee, you stop working because you are forced to retire when you reach a certain age. The idea of people becoming too old to work when they turn 60 is outdated and needs to be changed. Age is just a number. I am nearing 60, yet I find myself in the best physical and mental health, capable of doing the best job in my life. Just like it is illegal to discriminate against people on the grounds of caste, creed or gender, the laws should be made to stop discriminating against people based on their age. People should be retired only when they are physically and mentally unfit and incapable of doing their work efficiently.

Question: What is the best habit you've taken up from another person?
Answer: Around a year ago, I spent time with my daughter and son-in-law in Munich, Germany. The children used to go to the gym at 6 PM and would return by 7 PM. However, they would not take anything after the gym and would have dinner at 8.00 PM. Back home in India, we (me and my wife) also used to go to Gym between 6–7 PM. However, after returning from the gym, we felt hungry and would have high tea (tea with biscuits/snacks). We would then have our dinner at 9:00 PM. The result was that I was suffering from acidity and gas problems. However, we followed our children's routine in Munich and ate dinner early at 8.00 PM. In this way, we skipped one meal in the late evening and prepared our dinner in one hour. As a result, Therefore, we picked up this habit from our children and continue it today in India as well. You may also develop the habit of skipping evening snacks and having an early dinner. I am sure it will be good for your health and help you shed some weight. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: Why do almost all people think that they are good people?
Answer: A few days ago, when I was in Delhi for some personal work, I met one of my IRS batchmates in his office. We discussed the department (which I quit around 8 years ago), and then I casually mentioned the names of two senior retired officers I respected highly. My IRS friend was angry when I mentioned these officers’ names, and at one point in time, he got so angry that he said that he felt like hitting them hard or shooting them if they came before him. He then told me how he suffered in his career because of these two officers. I was amazed. I never thought that people whom I considered so good and professional could be so much hated by another colleague of mine. All people (not almost all) indeed think that they are good people. However, it is also true that there is no person in this world who is considered good by all people. If you don’t trust me, speak positively about anyone you consider the best person in the world, and rest assured that many people will criticise that person and hate him or her. For instance, I admire each of these people in the picture. However, you will find many people who hate and criticise them. Generally, we consider a person good if he is selfless and an evil person if he is selfish. However, selflessness and selfishness are complementary, as you have to first be selfish to do good to yourself, and then only you can be selfless to help others. Good and bad deeds are like credit and debit in the bank account. You can’t withdraw any money from the bank unless you deposit it first. Hence, in reality, good and bad complement each other, like yin and yang. For instance, if you wish to give charity (selfless), you must first earn money and create wealth for yourself (selfishness). However, when you create wealth for yourself, you are considered greedy and bad. The American author Elbert Hubbard once said, “To avoid criticism, do nothing, say nothing, be nothing." However, I can't entirely agree with him because even if you do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing, the world will still criticise you. If you judge a person's goodness from the perspective of others, you will never find a good person in the world. In the real world, even a bandit (like Valmiki) does the act of dacoity to feed his family, and a martyr of one person is a terrorist of another. Hence, just because some people consider you bad, you don’t cease to be a good person. Peter Drucker well said, “The idea that there are “well-rounded” people, people who have only strengths and no weaknesses (whether the term used is the “whole man,” the “mature personality,” the “well-adjusted personality,” or the “generalist”) is a prescription for mediocrity if not for incompetence. Strong people always have strong weaknesses too. When there are peaks, there are valleys.” If you want to see goodness, you can find them in every person. Otherwise, most people are quick to criticise everyone as evil to feel good and get a sense of superiority with all their evil. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: Why doesn't everyone dream big?
Answer: You perhaps know this man. He is Byju Raveendran, the founder of India’s highest-valued startup Byju’s. He dreamt big and founded ByJu’s, which was once valued at around $23 Billion. The company has raised over 5 billion [1]from investors and is now set to face an insolvency resolution process at the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). According to the Forbes Billionaire Index 2024, Raveendran’s net worth also went down to zero.[2]He is responsible for loosing 5 billion of investors wealth and is now being accused of cheating millions of students for not provinding them the promised qualityof education. You also perhaps know this man. His name is Arvind Kejriwal. A decade ago, he quit IRS and formed a political party called the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) to fight corruption in politics. He also dreamed big and became the Chief Minister of Delhi within months of forming his political party. Today, he is languishing in jail for several months for corruption. Many people in the world dream big. It is easy to dream big. It is, however, difficult to realise big dreams. Our dreams are nothing but our desires. When our desires are big, we are not satisfied even if we have enough wealth or power to live a happy life. The difference between our desires and reality creates a gap, which results in dissatisfaction and frustration that makes our lives miserable. Many people are willing to make all types of compromises, including breaking the social, moral and legal norms to realise their dreams. However, even if they realise their dreams, their past mischiefs don’t let them live in peace and catch up them very soon. Soon, they lose everything that they built over their lifetime and live a frustrated life. Our dreams should be realistic, and we should be able to achieve them with some effort without compromising our values and principles. We can keep raising the standards of our dreams if we attain our earlier dreams by fair means with a clear conscience. The most important thing is to live a happy and peaceful life, which does not require dreaming big and achieving great things. Big dreams are a euphemism for greed in the modern language, which are often the source of suffering and frustration rather than of happiness and peace. The German-American social psychologist and philosopher Erich Fromm wisely said, “Greed is a bottomless pit that exhausts the person in an endless effort to satisfy the need without ever reaching satisfaction.” It is good that everyone does not dream big, since that will only make the competition stiffer and realisation of dreams more difficult for everyone. It is also good for everyone that many people choose to remain happy with whatever they have rather than dream big, become greedy, and make their lives miserable in their attempt to fulfil their big dreams. Question: What impact does the bypassing of reservation system in lateral entry recruitment have on the representation of SC, ST, and OBC communities in higher administrative positions?
Answer: Lateral entry into civil services is not like a permanent appointment. These 'lateral entrants' are appointed on contracts for 3 years, which can be extended to a maximum of 5 years. [1] The appointment was to be made at the Deputy Secretary (DS) and Joint Secretary (DS) levels, which are already based on a selection basis, and there is no current reservation. It is also important to remember that these are secretariat postings where civil servants hardly enjoy any decision-making power, as almost all decisions in a ministry are taken at the level of the secretary and ministers. These lateral entry officers would only be making suggestions and helping the government formulate policies to bring in domain-specific expertise and fresh perspectives to enhance governance. I doubt if any sensible top-class experts would like to join the government for such non-executive temporary posts at government salaries, which will not be of any use to them when they go back to the corporate after 3/5 years. Even today, the representation of Scheduled Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) officers at the rank of joint secretary and secretary in the Government of India stands at 4% and 4.9%, respectively[2]against their reservation of 22.5% at the time of selection. It is pathetic to see the direction in which the reservation system in India is proceeding. The days are not far when caste-based reservations shall be demanded to appoint ministers and secretaries. Next, they will demand reservation when awarding government contracts to private parties or outsourcing any government work. It appears that the caste-based reservation shall not stop in India till the country is divided into thousands of categories and the ideal of equality and justice to all citizens is totally destroyed. Question: How can we protect our innocence and remain kind and open to trust others, when we are bombarded by manipulators and evil deeds that slowly change us?
Answer: Let me first tell you a story that shows the height of innocence. A saint was bathing in a river when he spotted a drowning scorpion. To help the scorpion he picked him up so that it could be set down on dry land. But as soon as the scorpion was picked he stung the saint’s hand and had to be dropped back in the water. The saint did not give up and tried again with the same result. This went on for a few more times when finally a passerby interrupted the saint, “Why do you keep doing this? Can’t you see the scorpion will sting you every time you try?” “The scorpion cannot forget its nature is to sting. But how can I forget that my nature is to love?” The saint replied.[1] While many people are impressed with this story that emphasises the importance of loving everyone including those who are your enemies, in my opinion this story shows the height of ignorance and stupidity. If instead of an scorpian a criminal comes to kill you or your loved one, will you still love him stating that it was his nature to kill, and it is my nature to love? In the real world, we must behave according to the situation. Accordingly, We also have the option for tit-for-tat with those who try to exploit us, by being evil to evil person and pay them in the same coin. However, this should be the last option and used only in exceptional cases, when the person is incorrigible and you can’t avoid them. Hence, instead of being good to everyone, like the saint of the story, you must learn to use judgement in every case and take the decisions depending on the person and the situation. Fortunately, according to my experience, most people in the world are good, and they don’t exploit others. You can be honest, kind and good to them and maintain your innocence. In the words of Chanakya — 'A person should not be too honest. Straight trees are cut first and honest people are screwed first.' It is wise to avoid all types of extremes, as extreme innocence and compassion is as much dangerous to a person as extreme manipulation and evil. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: What do you think is the most important factor for a successful and lasting relationship?
Answer: The most important factors for a lasting relationship are as follows. 1: Trust No relationship can last long if the partners don’t trust each other. It is important that we don’t ever break the trust with the person whom we love because trust, once broken, can never be repaired to its original status. It means that we must fulfil our promises, never be unfaithful to our spouse and never lie to our loved ones. 2: Responsibility Every relationship comes with a tacit responsibility. These responsibilities are not like a contract where every party has to state and agree on their duties and responsibilities, but something mutually agreed upon based on the social construct. For example, 3: Mutual Respect One of the most important requirements for a lasting relationship is mutual respect. All partners, like husband and wife, parents and children, and friends, must identify the good qualities in the other and respect each other. Many parents treat their children with little respect and expect their children to always respect them and be grateful for what they have done for them. Once children grow up, they must be treated more as friends than as children. Likewise, children often don’t respect their parents when they become more educated, spoiling relationships. No friendship can last without mutual respect, even if the partners' levels of education, wealth, and power may be very different. 4: Tolerance No two human beings can think identically. There have to be differences of opinions and beliefs between partners. One partner may believe in God, while the other may be an atheist. One partner may seek wealth and power, while the other may seek knowledge and peace. We have to learn to not only tolerate the differences but accept them by heart. Instead of telling the other that they are wrong, we must accept that there can be multiple perspectives on any issue. the attitude of ‘my-way-or-highway spoils all relationships. 5: Love You can never have a lasting relationship based on rationality alone since you will find your partner doing things that would be irrational in your opinion. Emotions are the glue for every lasting relationship, and a relationship without love becomes a burden sooner than later. When you love someone, the relationship becomes a joy, and you enjoy suffering for the sake of your loved one. The poem “I Love You, Mother” beautifully explains the secret of a lasting relationship. “I love you, Mother,” said little John, Then forgetting his work, his cap went on And off to the garden he went to the swing, Forgetting the coal and wood to bring. “I love you, Mother,” said little Nell, “I love you better than tongue can tell.” Then she teased and pouted full half the day So her mother rejoiced when she went out to play. “I love you, Mother,” said little Fan, “Today I’ll help you all I can; How glad I am that school doesn’t keep,” And she rocked the baby ’til it fell asleep. Then stepping softly she took the broom, And swept the floor and dusted the room. Happy and busy all day was she, As helpful and busy as a child could be. “I love you, Mother,” again they said, Three little children going to bed. How do you think that mother guessed Which one of them really loved her best?[1] Maintaining a lifelong relationship is as much an art as a science. You must learn to use your head and heart to forge and sustain a lasting relationship with any person, such as your spouse, children, parents, friends, colleagues, etc. I hope the suggestions discussed in the post will be useful in building a successful and lasting relationship. Question: Is it possible to live a happy life while being alone and single forever? Do some people believe this is their destiny?
Answer: If you get married, you are chained with numerous responsibilities. You have to take care of your spouse and children, which consumes a lot of your time and energy, leaving little time to follow your passion and achieve extraordinary success. On the other hand, if you are single, you can devote all your time and energy to your life's mission and achieve great success in the world. Many great personalities, such as Narendra Modi, Ratan Tata, Lata Mangeskar, Dr Kalam, and Rahul Gandhi, are examples of people who live happy and successful lives despite being single. However, for most ordinary people like us, it is difficult to enjoy happiness if you choose not to get married or have a partner. It is because we all wish to be loved and become special in some people’s lives. If you are single, you are special only to your parents, who gradually get old and die. After their death, your existence hardly matters in anyone’s life unless you choose to join the public life and devote your life to the public's good. However, when you get married, you become a special person for your spouse and children. You also achieve a lifelong purpose, as you can achieve happiness by making your loved one happy. Question: What are the differences between philosophy, science, religion, and spirituality in terms of seeking truth, knowledge, wisdom, and understanding?
Answer: While philosophy, science, religion, and spirituality seek the truth, their approaches differ. Let us understand their differences. Philosophy Philosophy is often called the love of wisdom. It asks fundamental questions like what is right and wrong, what is the purpose of life, how we should live, etc. It uses logic to answer these questions. For instance, based on logic and reason, it comes up with certain principles of ethics, like It proposes ideas that can improve your life and tells you what should be done. However, its principles are based on logic and not validated by empirical studies. Hence, there is no empirical study to prove that honesty is the best policy or that nonviolence is better than violence. In fact, it is easy to see that many dishonest people live better lives, and the most powerful people or countries are those that are violent. Science Earlier, all types of logical knowledge were called philosophy, and science was called ‘philosophy of nature’. When a philosophy is supported by empirical evidence, it becomes a science. Science tells you the reality as it is and not what reality should be. Science is very useful in understanding the natural phenomenon when inert matter is involved. However, in the matter of human beings, where the most cherished human goals like love, happiness, peace, and honour are not measurable, science is not helpful. Religion Religion is similar to philosophy as it also teaches us what is right and wrong, how we should live, what the purpose of life is, etc. However, unlike philosophy, it lacks a reason for developing its principles. Instead, it prescribes the same principles using the character of Gods and asks the people to follow them without question. Religion thus becomes a rigid philosophy since it can’t be questioned or changed with time. However, it provides stability, and it can be followed by everyone, unlike philosophy, which requires deeper knowledge of reason and logic. Spirituality Every religion has an infallible and omniscient God. However, there can only be one God and it can’t be different for all religions. In reality, the teachings of God in every religion are different. For instance, the Muslim God prohibits people from drinking alcohol, while a Christian God allows it. Hence, there is often conflict between people of different religions as they all believe in different truths. Spirituality is a broad concept with room for many perspectives, which includes a sense of connection to something bigger than ourselves, and it typically involves a search for meaning in life. As such, it is a universal human experience—something that touches us all.[1] A spiritual person believes in the concept of God, but not as it is mentioned in any particular religion. Instead, he ignores the conflicting opinions and tries to find the common truth among all religions to connect with God directly through his soul and imbibe the good qualities to become an ideal human being. Albert Einstein once said, “All religions, arts and sciences are branches of the same tree. All these aspirations are directed toward ennobling man's life, lifting it from the sphere of mere physical existence and leading the individual toward freedom.” Accordingly, while philosophy, religion, science, and spirituality are different in many ways, they all seek to find the truth and guide human beings to lead good and happy lives. They complement each other. Albert Einstein explained their mutual dependence by stating,“Science without religion is lame; religion without science is blind.” A wise human must have a philosophy in life, which he must follow religiously. However, he must never forgo his faculty of reason or develop blind faith in anything. Spirituality helps us combine these and realise our inner selves to choose our best path. Question: Is it appropriate for a teacher to share their personal feelings with students, such as having a bad day or feeling stressed at work?
Answer: A good teacher must connect with his students not only intellectually but also emotionally. When the students love their teachers, they learn best, while they fail to learn from those whom they hate. Plato, the Greek philosopher and the teacher of Aristotle, wisely said, “All learning has an emotional base." When a teacher shares his personal feelings with his students, he exposes his softer side to the students and gets their sympathy and empathy. By exposing his vulnerability, the teacher connects with the vulnerability felt by the students and then they developed some sort of bonding. In some strange way, this leads to an emotional connection between the teacher and student, leading to faster knowledge transmission. When a teacher becomes emotionally connected with students, teaching does not remain just a job to earn money but actually to make his students happy and more knowledgeable. The bond is similar to the bonding between the parents and the children. Just like parents would do anything for their children due to their emotional attachment to them, good teachers would also give their best when they love their students. I am making this statement based on my personal experience. When I was the course director of the IRS officers of the 2008 and 2009 batches, I used to share my personal experiences with the IRS probationers, which helped me develop a great emotional connection with them. Accordingly, I was awarded the WCO Certificate of Merit in 2011 for my work at the National Academy of Customs Excise and Narcotics (NACEN). Many IRS probationers were present at the award function. Hence, when my name was called for the award (Watch this video at 3.00 minutes), there was so much clapping that you won’t be able to hear any announcement made by the anchor about me. Likewise, when I used to teach Ethics and essay courses at Unacademy, I used to share many personal stories (personal and professional) with them. As a result, even though I was teaching online and I could not see their faces, I interacted with them through the chat facility and developed great emotional connections. The result was that I always developed excellent rapport with my students, who loved my class. I received a 99% overall rating on my teaching. However, we must be careful while sharing our feelings with them and maintain utmost dignity in conversation. Our personal experiences and anecdotes must not digress from the subject but must be used to provide credibility to the subject by providing real-life experience—and what can be better than our own experiences? We don’t differentiate between knowledge and the knower. Accordingly, if the students like a teacher, they shall also love the subject and learn it better and faster.

Question: Is “sometimes I get mad” a valid justification for ripping someone’s ears off?
Answer: The question reminds me of a conversation I had with my wise boss a few years ago when we were discussing human relationships. He suddenly asked me, ‘Suppose I give you a glass of almond (badam) milk flavoured with kesar (saffron). Would you like to drink it?’ ‘Most certainly, yes, Sir. I love badam milk.’ ‘Now suppose that you are sitting in an open restaurant, and just before you take the first slip of the milk, a bird sitting on the tree drops its excrement in the milk. Can you still drink it?’ ‘That will be horrible, Sir. It will be impossible to drink such milk’, I replied, twisting my face in disgust. He then gave the following words of wisdom, which can be paraphrased as following. ‘Beautiful relationships are like milk filled with almonds and saffron. We make great efforts to create relationships with our spouses, parents, children, or friends. We do everything for them, take care of them, and say numerous complimentary things to them because we love them from the bottom of our hearts. Then, one day, when we are low or upset, or our loved one commits some mistake, we lose our temper and shout at them. We say something to them, or do something that hurt them badly. After some time, when we are sober, we feel bad and even profusely apologize. Yet just like a drop of bird dropping is sufficient to spoil millions of drops of milk, our one wrong action damages the relationship very badly, forever. The hurt person on the receiving end does not remember our hundred good deeds and words but remembers every harsh word uttered by us, or physical harm done by us when we lost our temper. It takes a lifetime to build a relationship, but just a second to break it forever. If we can just control ourselves on those few moments, we can always have a deep and fulfilling relationship with our loved ones.’ Our values are tested not so much when everything is going fine, but when we are under tremendous pressure, or lose our temper. You shall be judged as the type of person who had been in the worst case and not in the best case. If you behave badly when you get mad, like ripping off someone’s ear in anger, all your good deeds shall be forgotten, and you shall be identified by your worst deeds only. Life-long relationships can be broken, and lifetime good work can be overshadowed by just one bad action. Occasional anger is not bad, but we have to learn to get angry in the right way. Aristotle wisely said, “Anybody can become angry—that is easy, but to be angry with the right person and to the right degree and at the right time and for the right purpose, and in the right way—that is not within everybody's power and is not easy.” Hence, it is important to control anger and not say or do anything in a fit of anger, for which we have to repent for life, and yet we won’t be able to reverse the damage. Question: Will the government make creamy layers applicable to SC/ST after the recent Supreme Court judgment?
Answer: The Supreme Court's judgement regarding the concept of a creamy layer is welcome, as it reduces the injustice within SC/STs. However, the judgement is not unanimity but delivered with the majority of 4:3. Further, the judgement is advisory in nature and does not bend on the government. Justice BR Gavai, in his judgment, said, "The State must evolve a policy for identifying the creamy layer even from the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes so as to exclude them from the benefit of affirmative action. In my view, only this and this alone can achieve the real equality as enshrined under the Constitution." He also stated that it was appropriate to consider the issue of the creamy layer since the Court is dealing with the question of equality among the group of unequal. Furthermore, the judgement also allowed the sub-classification of Scheduled Castes to give separate quotas to most backward classes.[1] This judgement may be good from the point of justice within the SC/ST since, at present, most of the reservation is cornered by the creamy layer within each category. However, it will make the reservation system more complex, prone to corruption and deteriorate the quality of government institutions. Already the quality of the SC/ST candidates getting admission into top colleges in India and getting government job is poor compared to OBC or the unreserved category. If this judgement is implemented, the quality of the candidates in the academic institution is likely to decline drastically, as most of the better students within each category would be excluded from the reserved category. Reservation is a bad idea which divides society, reduces the quality of every institution and fails to give equality and justice enshrined in the Constitution. Imagine that the creamy layer is set at an annual income of Rs 8 lakhs. Can you say that SC/ST students whose parents earn 1 lakh and those who earn 8 lakhs are equal? And if your income becomes 8.01 lakhs, you lose all reservation benefits. Hence, though this judgement will debar some SC/ST people whose parents are well off, it will neither promote equality nor improve the efficiency of government departments or the quality of education. Most likely, the government will implement the judgement since it will get them the support of at least 90% of SC/STs who will benefit from the exclusion of the creamy layer from the ambit of reservation.

Question: What are some reasons why people may not want their children to become IAS officers? Is being an IAS officer still considered a prestigious career in our country?
Answer: The prestige of IAS or other civil services, like IPS, IRS, and IFS, depends on which society you come from. Accordingly, if you have lived mostly in a metropolitan city and were brought up in a metropolitan culture, your children may not prefer to join the civil services for the following reasons. 1: Cost-Benefit Analysis The competition for IAS is very tough. Almost one million candidates apply for less than 1000 seats in civil services, and the chances of selection are just 1/1000. If you specifically aim for IAS, you should be in the top 100; hence, the chances are 1/10,000. The average age of selection is 27 years. If you are not selected, your alternative career is almost finished. Hence, most young people don’t consider it worthwhile to take so much risk, and struggle so much for a job. 2: Personal Life In IAS, your postings are generally in small places for most of your career where the children may not get good schools. Further, you can be transferred anytime, hence the family lack peace and stability. If your spouse is working (including in civil services), you may spend most of your time in separate stations and can’t enjoy good family life. Purely, from family life perspective, the IAS/IPS are designed for single spouse working and the other spouse being a housemaker, so they can move together any time on transfer. Hence, these services suits male officers who marry housemakers (as Lady officers dont prefer househusbands). Family life is difficult for the rest. The central services like IRS, suites more to the working couples as the transfer policy provides for giving preference to posting on the station of spouse. 3: Salary Structure The salaries in the top corporate jobs are now much better than the IAS officers. An IAS officer with, say, 20 years of seniority may be getting around Rs 200,000 pm, while the top salaries in corporate may be up to 10 times as much. The salary of an IAS officer increases only by 3% per year (plus DA), however hard you work and however good you are at your work. In corporate, you can reach to become the CEO when you are merely 40 years old. 4: Corruption Government services are known for corruption. While a corrupt officer can indeed make lots of money, he can hardly sleep peacefully because, if he is caught, he goes to jail, and all his prestige goes to the drain. If you choose to be honest, you can hardly live as lavishly as your corporate counterparts. You also can’t save enough money to ensure a good returned life, particularly if you joined the service after 2004, i.e. after the new pension scheme was introduced. The worst thing is that you may face frequent transfers if you work honestly at every assignment, like Ashok Khemka, IAS. [1] 5: Polticial interference Gone are the days when IAS officers enjoyed real power and could exercise it using their best judgment. Such officers are hardly tolerated in modern times. If you wish to get good postings and enjoy power, be ready to listen to politicians and accept political interference. Sometimes, you have to even cook food to please your poltical bosses.[2] Unfortunately, politicians won’t rescue you if you get into trouble since you signed all the files and made the decisions. Hence, if you are a brilliant student today, you have many other career options that may be better than IAS. Hence, it is unsurprising that most children of civil servants now like to work in the top corporations in India or get a job in Western countries where they get a much better quality of life and excellent career prospects. Question: Are you in agreement with the political saying that absolute political power corrupts politics absolutely?
Answer: Imagine you are the real Emperor with absolute power, like Marcus Aerulous, Ashoka or Akbar. Do you think you will ever engage in any form of corruption? An absolute power means the ruler can do anything without facing consequences. In practical terms, it means, If you indeed have such power, why would you engage in corruption? We can accuse the world's emperors of anything, but we can’t call them corrupt. Just like you can’t steal your own money, you can’t be corrupt if you have absolute ownership of everything. Corruption happens when you don’t have absolute power but enjoy only part of it for a limited salary. Let us take the examples of corruption in government. Suppose you are a powerful officer, like a District Collector, Superintendent of Police, Tax Commissioner officer or civil servant, and the law gives you the (absolute) power to conduct a search, seize properties and arrest a person violating the law. However, such a legislative power is never absolute since the power lies with the chair and not on you. Hence, you can be transferred, and all powers can be taken away from you in no time. Let me give more specific examples. Suppose I am a tax Commissioner. I conduct a raid against powerful businessmen and detect a case of tax evasion amounting to one billion (100 crores) rupees. Do I get an extra salary or a faster promotion due to recovering such a huge amount of money? The answer is NO. Suppose the businessman is close to the politicians in power and spends a few million rupees; he can transfer me within days and post me into some insignificant charge where I will have NIL power. On the other side, I can make money from corruption if I negotiate with the businessman and make a few million for not conducting a raid. Now, imagine that he gets 10% of the the tax recovery as rewards and protection from transfer. Will he not be do his job more honestly? Since, as a public servant, you neither enjoy absolute power nor enjoy unlimited income. Hence, there is corruption. You may think that the top politicians, like Chief Ministers, prime Ministers, or Presidents in some countries, enjoy absolute power and are hence very corrupt. In reality, even these top politicians don’t enjoy absolute power, as the people can change them in the next election, causing them to lose all their power. Hence, these politicians have to make a lot of illegal money through corruption to spend during elections to retain power. Hence, the relationship between power and corruption can be presented in the following Bell curve. In the curve, the power is represented on the X-axis, while corruption is represented on the Y-axis. Let us understand that corruption refers to misusing public power for personal gain. [1] When all the powers are already vested in you (and the public has no power), nothing you do can be considered corruption.

Question: Why do brides cry on their wedding day when they move with their grooms even though they feel happy?
Answer: When I was young, we used to spend our summers in the village. In those days, most of the marriages used to take place in summers. Hence, I had the opportunity to attend several weddings in villages. I remember the wedding of my two buas (aunts) as a young child. Both the aunts were quite gloomy during the entire wedding and weeping profusely at the time of their vidai (bride’s farewell). In fact, my younger bua fainted at the time of bidai. Even when my younger sister got married 30 years ago, everyone in the family was weeping profusely at the time of bidai. However, when my daughters got married a few years ago, there was no crying at the time of bidai, either by the bride or by the family member. In fact, the bride and groom danced as a couple at the sangeet ceremony a day before, and they both enjoyed the entire marriage ceremony. In the past, the bride used to cry because they used to be quite nervous at their wedding as they had to leave their parents' house and go to her Sasural (In-law’s place), where she did not know anyone, including the husband. In the past, the sasural used to be a dreaded place for brides, as the expectations from the bride were very high. At the time of muh-dekhai (watching the face of the bride), she often used to face very uncomplimentary remarks from the village women about her complexion and beauty. It was common for the bride to hear remarks from the in-law family about the dowery and jewellery. She was supposed to know all household jobs like cooking, knitting, cleaning etc. She was to cook food normally on the first or second day to prove her cooking skills. She had to sign songs in the functions. If she had been found lacking, she would have had to hear numerous indictments from her in-law family, and negative things about her parents. All that used to be very painful for the young bride. The worst thing in the past was that the girl’s parents used to wash off their hands after the wedding, and there was no possibility of divorce or coming back to their parent’s house after the marriage. Naturally, the brides used to be tense, nervous, and apprehensive at their wedding, as their lives were to be transformed forever. However, in modern times, most weddings in the cities are love marriages, where the bride and groom have known each other for several months or years. Moreover, the culture of dowery has been almost eliminated in the case of love marriages. Since the bride and groom are financially independent, their groom’s parents would not be able to tease or humiliate the bride. The best thing is that in modern times, most parents don’t differentiate between boys and girls. They always stand with the girl before and after marriage, and she knows that in case of any problems, her parents will always be there for her. As a result, modern brides genuinely feel happy during the wedding and enjoy the entire function. Instead of crying, she laughs, dances and goes happily to her in-law's place. However, in villages and semi-urban areas, arranged marriages still take place in the old traditional ways, and the brides still face the same problems. Hence, it is not surprising that such brides would be crying profusely at the time of their wedding due to the uncertainty and fear of mistreatment at their in-law's place. Question: Have any IAS or IPS officers resigned due to corruption charges? If so, what were their names and positions at the time of resignation?
Answer: If a civil servant, such as an IAS or IPS officer, resigns due to corruption charges, his resignation will not be accepted. It is important to understand that quitting the government is not a right for a government officer. If you resign from your job when a vigilance case or a department enquiry is pending against you, the resignation will not be accepted until you are cleared in the enquiry. For instance, Mr Shah Faesal (IAS topper of the 2010 batch) tendered his resignation from the Indian bureaucracy in protest on 9 January 2019, citing "unabated killings" in Kashmir, among other things. However, the central government "never accepted" his resignation, and he had to withdraw it later. Currently, he is posted as Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Culture.[1] Similarly, Kannan Gopinathan (IAS), resigned from the job in 2019 to express his anger over what happened in Kashmir. His resignation has not yet been accepted, as departmental enquiries against him are still pending, and he continues to be in government service. Hence, an IAS or IPS officer can’t resign if he or she is facing corruption charges until he or she is cleared of them. If they are not cleared of the corruption charges, they will be dismissed from their jobs and jailed rather than allowed to quit civil services. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: Is all fair in love and war?

Hence, when we are able to attack, we must seem unable; when using our forces, we must appear inactive; when we are near, we must make the enemy believe we are far away; when far away, we must make him believe we are near.” In war, winning is important since it is a question of your survival. Hence, it can be said that everything is fair in war. In the case of love, you have to win the beloved's heart. Love can never last long if you win her heart by unfair means like cheating, deception, lying or fraud. Hence, everything is not fair in love, and you must follow the highest level of moral and ethical values in case of love. Otherwise, you may win her body, but you can never win her heart and never get true love.

So you always needed a driver for your cars, which also cost a lot of money. Around 1986, the Indian government, in collaboration with Suzuki, started manufacturing the “Maruti 800’, which was self-driven and required little maintenance. Suddenly, you needed no driver to drive your cars, as most people started driving the cars themselves. Over the next four decades, many car companies started producing cars in India that are almost maintenance-free and self-driven. As a result, the number of cars has grown exponentially, and by 2022, India will have more than 70 million (7 crore) cars.[1] I estimate that more than 90% of the cars are self-driven. Does it mean that the development of such cars has taken the jobs of more than 63 million drivers? It is well said that no one can stop the idea whose time has come. When computers were introduced in the 1980s, it was feared that they would take away the jobs of many people. Indeed, computers have reduced the need for manpower and are organisations are able to deliver services much more economically and efficiently. The advent of the internet further revolutionised the work in every organisation. Question: Has the teaching profession gained more respect over time or does it still lack respect from society members? What are the reasons for this?
Answer: When I was in my intermediate class (11–12) in Government Jublie Inter College (Lucknow), we used to have a physics teacher, G C Saxena, who was so brilliant that before a student completed his doubt, he would start solving the problems. I have never found him stuck up in any problem, even the most difficult problems of IIT-JEE. Unfortunately, our chemistry teacher was not good. However, another chemistry teacher, Mr K P Srivastava, was known to be an excellent teacher at the college. He used to teach chemistry in another section. His voice was so loud that you could hear his lecture from the corridor. He was always ready to help us. So, we used to get his help in solving complex problems and understanding difficult chemistry concepts, and he was always ready to help. The teachers then lived simple lives and came to school on scooters or bicycles. When I went to IIT(BHU) Varanasi for my B Tech, there were many excellent teachers. Many of them got their higher degrees in the USA and chose to teach in India. Some of them were so simple that they used to come on bicycles. A teacher is known due to his knowledge and not how he lives and which vehicle he uses to travel from one place to another. A few years back, I met some UPSC educators at an online UPSC seminar, to which I was also invited. While I attended the seminar in my humble Hyundai Xcent, other UPSC educators came in luxurious cars with drivers. Two educators had high-end Mercedes models, costing above one crore rupee. One educator was hardly 35 years old. During our discussion, another educator, who was still in their early 30s and unmarried, told me he had an expensive house in Delhi and was constructing a farmhouse at a hill station near Kasauli. The people of this generation may not believe that tuition and coaching were considered an enigma in the past, and only the very weak students used to join coaching. Most of my batchmates in IIT or Civil Services never joined any coaching to succeed in the competition. Unfortunately, coaching has become one of India's biggest industries and knowledge factories. The coaching industry's market revenue in India in 2022 was Rs 58,088 crore, and it was projected to reach Rs 1,33,995 crore rupees by 2028.[1] The best teachers in coaching institutes earn crores, many times more than the teachers of schools, colleges, and even the top-notch institutes in India. Similarly, the top students of IITs, IIMs, and other prestigious institutes earn salaries today that are higher than those of senior professors and even directors of these institutes. As a result, the quality of teachers in colleges and academic institutions has declined. Hence, it is unsurprising that teachers are generally not respected as much as they used to be. In fact, in modern times, teachers are often not even accepted as Gurus (who used to be considered higher than even Gods earlier) but treated as service providers who must deliver the best services (knowledge) in consideration of the money paid by the consumers (students). Conversely, if you don’t have money, you will have no option but to work outside in the hot summers and chilly winters with inadequate clothes to earn your living which is sure to make your life miserable. If you have money, you can avoid such jobs at such times and choose to work (or not work) that are pleasant and make you happy. While things pertaining to external dimensions require money to buy, all the money in the world can’t buy contentment, wisdom, knowledge, or love, which, too, are necessary to complete the circuit of happiness. Hence, wealth is necessary but not a sufficient condition for happiness. If you find some of the wealthiest people leading miserable lives, it is not due to their wealth, but because they earned money illegally or immorally, or in the process of earning money, they sacrificed the things that pertain to the internal dimensions (which money can’t buy), like honesty, love, compassion, and contentment. Question: Was Osho a fraud? How much of what he says is relevant?
Answer: Osho was a brilliant and knowledgeable person. He understood the human mind like no one else in recent times. He also has tremendous persuasive skills and a command of the language, both Hindi and English. His audio and videos are still viral, and they are shared frequently on all social media platforms. The most interesting thing is that he used reason and logic to persuade people. However, when you probe deeper, you discover that he was the master of logical fallacies and used invalid logic to convince people. His strategy was twofold. Osho was good at demolishing other people’s ideas, but his ideas were even worse. They may lead you nowhere or take you to prison or a life of disgrace. Let me discuss some of his most famous quotes with you and point out their fallacies. The OSHO website [1]provides some of Osho's most famous quotes. Let me discuss a few of them to expose their fallacies. 1: No Philosopher Has Ever Been Able to Know the Truth Quote: “No philosopher has ever been able to know the truth. All the philosophers have been thinking about the truth. But thinking about the truth is an impossibility. Either you know it, or you don't.” Fallacy: Scientific methods have been able to find numerous truths and the laws of nature using rationality. Truth is not an either/or thing. It may be infinite, like the universe, but even its partial knowledge has transformed human society. 2: Love Should Be like Breathing Quote: “Love should be like breathing. It should be just a quality in you wherever you are, with whomsoever you are. Even if you are alone, love goes on overflowing from you. It is not a question of being in love with someone – it is a question of being love.” Fallacy: No reason is provided that a human being can become loved. You love people when they are lovable and possess the quality that is worth loving. You can’t love an enemy or some who is trying to destroy you. How can you love an unfaithful spouse, a rapist and a terrorist? 3: Trust Has Nothing to Do with the Object of Trust Quote: “Trust is unconditional. It simply says that, ‘I have that quality which trusts. Now, it is irrelevant what happens to my trust – whether it is respected or not, whether it is deceived or not. That is not the point at all.’ Trust has nothing to do with the object of trust, it has something to do with your inner quality: can you trust?” Fallacy: Trust is never unconditional. Only a dumb person can trust everyone. Can you trust a liar, fraud or criminal? We can trust only those who are worthy of trust because they speak truth and follow honesty and integrity in life. If you carefully listen to Osho’s lectures, you can easily find that they either lack any logic or are full of logical fallacies. Unfortunately, most people lack critical thinking skills. They can’t differentiate between valid and invalid arguments, and hence, they fall for Osho's fallacious arguments. Many people consider him as enlightened as Buddha, while others think that he was a fraud. I believe there is no comparison between Gautam Buddha and Osho (Rajneesh). It is no wonder that Osho was accused of various criminal charges in America. Under the deal his lawyers made with the U.S. Attorney's office, he was given a ten-year suspended sentence, five years' probation, and a $400,000 penalty in fines and prosecution costs and agreed to leave the United States, not returning for at least five years without the permission of the U.S. Attorney General.[3] If you want to know more about his rise and fall, watch the Netflix documentary "Wild Wild Country.”[4] If you know all about him, it is not difficult to decide whether he was an enlightened guru or a fraud. His lectures have no logic, or he uses invalid logic to prove his point. However, he is a pleasure to listen to as he entertains and speaks what you wish to listen to, and it is easy to get addicted to his speeches and reels. No wonder he has millions of admirers and followers several decades after his death.

This naturally means a commitment of time and money. Many people, instead of fulfilling their social obligation towards their friends, make some excuse to avoid the commitment. Similarly, when our friend or their family members are in trouble, it is our duty to help them, even without asking. If you don’t stand up for your friends when they need you the most, you can’t hope to have good friends in your life. Such people are soon exposed, and they lose not only the friend whom they refuse to help but every other person who now understands their true character. Thomas Aquinas wisely said, “There is nothing on this earth more to be prized than true friendship.” However, there are no free lunches in the world. Friendship is not only a privilege but also a huge commitment. If you wish to have good friends, be ready to pay the price by always fulfilling your commitments as a friend, and never leave a friend in need. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: Was India better before or now?
Answer: India is far better now than ever before. Today’s India is far more just, equitable, prosperous, and educated than ever. In earlier times, war was the only solution to disputes between influential people, such as kings. Today, we have fair laws and courts to adjudicate disputes. For instance, Ram was to be sent to Vanwas (Stay in the forest) for 14 years because, in those days, the laws were such that the eldest son would inherit the kingdom, while the other sons would practically get nothing, and they had to always work under their elder brothers. Hence, Kaikeyee was concerned that her son “Bharat’ would get nothing. Hence, she used her influence over Dashrath to give throne to his son Bharat and send Ram to the forest. This situation would never arise today because modern law gives all brothers and sisters equal rights. Similarly, the war of Mahabharath was basically a property dispute which would have never taken place if the modern system of the rule of law and courts had been there. In modern times, the average person is far more educated than people in the past, when the privilege of education was vested only to the selected few. In the past, the lower caste people were not even allowed to get an education, while today, every Indian, irrespective of their caste and creed, has the same right to education. The greatest beneficiaries of modern values are women, who constitute half of the population but hardly had any rights in the past. Today, there is nothing that a woman can’t do. She has equal rights as men, and can achieve anything in the world if they have the will and determination. They can become the head of state and occupy the posts of Prime Minister or President of the country. (Picture above: Angela Merkel, Jacinda Ardern, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Indira Gandhi, Margaret Thatcher)[1] The advancement of medical science has improved life expectancy, and people are living almost 70 years today as compared to less than 30 years at the time of independence. Most people think that India was better in the ancient period because they are unaware of the problems of the past and take the benefits of the modern world for granted. However, on rational analysis, we can easily conclude that India, like any other country in the world, is far better today than ever before. Today is the best time to be born in India; hopefully, tomorrow will be even better.

Question: I have given 4 attempts at civil services but couldn't even clear the prelims. Even after working so hard each and every time I cant clear the exam. Now I have started feeling lost and confused about what should I do?
Answer: If you could not clear UPSC prelims even after 4 attempts, you must seriously reconsider your decision to write civil services. I agree that civil services are unpredictable, but like any other examination, it tests your knowledge of the subject, and it requires a certain type of aptitude and ability to clear the examination. If you fail to make it to the top 10,000 in India, there are very weak chances of making it to the top 800 to get an appointment as a civil servant. While there are a few exceptional cases where an aspirant is able to make it to the final list, even after failing four times in prelims, these are the rarest of the rare. I would suggest that you start exploring other career options, like the PCS, banking or a job in the private sector, instead of exhausting all your attempts and becoming overage. Please don’t follow in the footsteps of UPSC aspirant Mr Kunal R Virulkar, who wrote 12 attempts, 7 mains, 5 interviews, and NO SELECTION.[1] He might have received a lot of sympathy from the people, but he can’t get back almost 14-15 years of his precious life, which he wasted on his dream of becoming a civil servant. Don’t forget that he was a better student than you because he cleared prelims 7 times in his 12 attempts. After working in the IRS for over 25 years and closely knowing my friends in IAS, IPS, IFS, etc., I can say that taking too much risk for civil services is not worth it. At the end of the day, the civil services is just another job with its own pros and cons. Hence, be realistic and don’t waste your life chasing something that is not worth so many precious years of your life and future.

Question: Do you think that income inequality is bad for social cohesion? Why or why not?
Answer: Let us start with the inequality prevailing on Quora itself. There are over 400 million monthly Quora users. [1]Millions of people write answers on Quora, but most views are cornered by just a few people. For instance, as of today, These top writers on Quora get hundreds of thousands of views and several thousand upvotes in a single day, while millions of other Quora users don’t get as much traction even in their lifetime. I am sure that if Quora implements such an equitable policy, it will lose all its popularity. It will cause the best writers to lose interest in writing and the most avid readers to lose interest in reading. It is important to understand that in a free market society, the people are awarded based on their performance. They get benefits in proportion to their contributions to society. The most important thing is that the benefit to society is far more than the benefit to the individual. Let me illustrate this with an example. Suppose, currently a product A available on the market for $100. Now, Mr X, create a new product after spending $1 billion to develop a better product B, and make it available at $50 only. Now, imagine that 100 million people buy the product and thus save more than $5 billion. Now, businessman X gets $25 net earnings on each sale, and thus, he corners $2.5 billion for himself. Hence, after adjusting his cost of $1 billion, he still makes $1.5 billion for himself. In this example, businessman X made a net profit of $1.5 billion, while conumers get a billion dollar product for jusr $ 50, and save $50 for buying such product, compared to past. Do you think the profit Mr X earns is bad for society? Do you think the inequality Mr X created is bad for social cohesion? In fact, society is indebted to Mr X since, due to him, millions of people can now afford a product that they could not have afforded if it was priced $100. Furthermore, they will spend their $50 savings on buying something else, which will not only create more demand for products in the world but also make their lives better. Because of such individuals, the world's total wealth increases every year, and the pie grows bigger. The below figure illustrates the Gross World Product, CE-1–2015. According to the source “Our World in Data, Roser 2016c, based on data from the World Bank and from Angus Maddison and Maddison Project 2014”, global wealth multiplied by 1700 times between the years 1700 and 2015 (from the book Pinker, Steven. Enlightenment Now (p. 81). Penguin Books Ltd). Hence, even if the wealthiest people are getting wealthier, huge benefits are also accruing to the poorest people in the world. Even a profit of $1.5 billion earned by Mr X will improve the world since almost half of it may be collected by the Government in the form of personal income tax, corporate tax, and indirect taxes. Even with the remaining money, he will buy something like a house, car, etc., which will ultimately create more demand for goods, provide more employment, and raise taxes for the government. When the government collects more taxes, it can spend more money on social welfare schemes, free healthcare, education, etc., which will help the poor and reduce inequality by raising the standards of living of the poorest people in society. It is a fact that inequality motivates writers to create the best content for users by doing extensive research and learning from the best writers on Quora or other platforms. Similarly, income inequality is why people work hard to learn, create and innovate new products for society. No one is going to slog if everyone is going to get the same benefits. However, in the process, everyone benefits in society. Ultimately, the consumer or the reader is the king because he or she decides what to buy, read, and like. Their choice determines what the entrepreneurs or writers would create. Merit-based inequality thus creates a strong bond between writers and readers and between innovators and users. The grateful world indeed pays homage to such innovators and creators. The picture below shows the tribute paid to Steve Jobs, a top entrepreneur and one of the richest persons of his time.[2] Hence, if societal inequality arises based on performance and merit, it is good for the individuals and society. Inequality becomes bad only when people acquire wealth, power, or other advantages by illegal or immoral means.

Question: Why did Hindutva not work well this time for BJP & Modi? Is it due to new found unity among the opposition parties or did the low percentage of voting as such helped the I.N.D.I.A?
Answer: “You can fool some of the people all of the time and all of the people some of the time, but you can not fool all of the people all of the time.” This famous quote from Abraham Lincoln explains the defeat of the BJP in Uttar Pradesh. The Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanathsaid claimed before the election that the Samajwadi Party (SP) would fail to open its account in the 2024 Lok Sabha election and that all the five members of the party’s first family were set to lose.[1] However, after the election, BJP has to eat the humble pie. The BJP's national vote share fell from 37.3 percent in 2019 to 36.6 percent in 2024, which is not very significant. But, the BJP lost 63 seats (from 303 to 240), because the INDIA alliance helped consolidate the opposition votes in many places. [3] This happened when opposition parties were not fully united, and their votes split in most parts of India. Thus, it is evident that if opposition parties are united, the BJP has no chance of winning a majority in the Parliament. The BJP’s success has been largely due to its divide-and-rule strategy, which divided the Indians on a communal basis and ensured that the opposition parties didn’t come together by using the ED, CBI, and Income Tax departments. While Modi has become the PM for the third time, the interesting thing is that this time, it is the NDA government in the centre and not the Modi Government, where Modi enjoyed absolute power due to his absolute majority in parliament. I hope the results of the 2024 elections will bring some sanity to the rank and files of the BJP and Shri Modi and make them respect the opinions and ideologies of more than 63% of Indians who have not voted for them as they don’t accept their Hindutva agenda in politics.

Question: How does luck play its role in life?
Answer: “There are only two ways to live your life”, said Albert Einstein. “One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.” We can use the quote to describe luck as well, “There are two ways to look at the role of ' luck’ in life. One is that there is nothing like ‘luck’, and the other is that everything is ‘luck’. Many people believe that everything in the world depends on luck and that we are helpless creatures playing in the hands of destiny. They insist that our lives depend on luck because all the factors responsible for our success (or failure) are a matter of luck. These factors include, We can see easily that we have little control over these factors. Hence, if you are lucky, you are born with all the right attributes that make you successful (High intelligence, a wealthy and loving family, a good college, a developed country, good looks, etc. ). Similarly, if you are simply unlucky if you are born in all unfavourable conditions. Hence, according to this view, life is like a lottery, and you are simply lucky if you are happy, successful and wealthy. However, in my opinion, it is not significant that you are born with many perks, but more important is how you use these benefits to shape your life. If you fail to use the benefits correctly, they may become a curse to you, instead of making your life happier. For instance, Most importantly, what looks like a great gift to a person may turn out to be his greatest liability in different conditions. A horse is certainly considered to be more gifted than an ass, but it does not mean that he is more lucky, as evident from the following Aesop’s Fable. A Horse and an Ass were travelling together, the Horse prancing along in its fine trappings, the Ass carrying with difficulty the heavy weight in its panniers. “I wish I were you,” sighed the Ass; “nothing to do and well fed, and all that fine harness upon you.” The next day, however, there was a great battle, and the Horse was wounded to death in the final charge of the day. His friend, the Ass, happened to pass by shortly afterwards and found him on the point of death. “I was wrong,” said the Ass.[1] Hence, our lives depend on what we think, say, and do, rather than what we are born with or what we acquire through luck or chance. The gains by luck are similar to the gains by tossing the coin, which eventually even out. Ultimately, our life depends on our own hard work, sincerity, commitment and grit. The former American president Thomas Jefferson said aptly, “I’m a great believer in luck, and I find the harder I work, the more I have of it.” We are the makers of our own lives and creators of our own luck and destiny.
