Question: Richard Feynman said, “Never confuse education with intelligence, you can have a PhD and still be an idiot.” What are some real life examples of this?
Answer: Intelligence is generally defined as the ability to gather knowledge and skills and apply them to your life to solve life's complex problems. On the other hand, education requires you to get into a college and pass the examination prescribed by law to get the required degree. If you have a good memory and follow rote learning, you can easily get even the highest degree in the world with top marks. Getting a degree has become so easy in modern times that anyone with average intelligence can acquire any degree, including a PhD, provided he or she is willing to spend the desired time pursuing the degree. Most PhD holders work in universities, where a PhD is the minimum requirement to become a faculty member. However, many professors are people of average intelligence who often choose the teaching profession not as a matter of choice but because they did not get into the best jobs at their lower qualifications. Smarter people often get jobs after their BE/B Tech, MBA, LLB/LLM, MBBS/MS, etc., and have better career prospects. The smartest people don’t waste their time doing graduation but drop out of school and college and set up companies like Microsoft, Apple or Google. The wisest people in the world, like Buddha, Kabir, or Socrates did not have a college degree, but they learned their lessons from life itself using their analytical skills and keen observation. While education is helpful in acquiring knowledge, it does not make you more intelligent. Knowledge acquired from textbooks can make an intelligent person wiser and more creative, but it can also make a stupid person even more stupid. The story of ‘Four Learned Fools’ from Panchtantra illustrates how education can’t make a stupid person intelligent. In a town, there lived four friends who were quite learned. One day, they decided to leave their native place and seek their fortune in the city, which offered so many more opportunities to earn money. Packing in all their holy books, they were on their way.[1] Soon, they came to an intersection of the road and did not know which path to follow. Now, the son of a merchant had died in the town, and at that very moment, a huge funeral procession that included several prominent citizens of the town passed by. One of the friends consulted his holy scriptures and read aloud: ‘Whichever road is followed by great men is the right one to follow’. So they said, ‘Let us go the same way as these people.’ Following the road taken by the prominent citizens, the group reached the cremation ground, and saw a donkey standing there. The second friend opened his holy scriptures and read: ‘Whosoever stands by you on all occasions, whether joyous or sad, is your true friend’. So, the four friends concluded that the donkey was their true friend. Accordingly, one of the friends put his arms around the donkey’s neck; the second friend kissed him, whilst the third began to wash his hoofs. They kept chanting, ‘He is our true friend’. Just then, they saw a camel advance quickly towards them. The third friend consulted his religious book and read: ‘Righteousness marches rapidly.’ So they all agreed that the advancing camel must be nothing but righteousness incarnate. Right then, the fourth friend opened his holy scriptures and read: ‘A wise man should lead his friend to righteousness’. So they decided to introduce the donkey to the camel, and when the camel approached, they tied the two animals together. When the donkey’s master, a washerman, heard the news that his donkey was being dragged along by a camel, he picked up a stick to beat the four learned fools, who then had to run for their lives. When they had gone a little way, the foursome came upon a river. The leaf of a holy tree was floating by. One of them cried, ‘This holy leaf will take us across the river.’ And with this, he jumped on it and immediately began to drown. Then, another friend caught him by the neck. However, the friend recalled certain words of wisdom: ‘When total destruction is imminent, a wise man sacrifices half and works with the rest.’ So he concluded, ‘He should be cut into two!’ And they cut the friend they had saved into two halves with a sharp sword and moved on. [2] It is easy to see that these learned fools had all the right knowledge, but they did not know how to use it correctly to solve real-life problems. So, Richard Feynman is right. A highly educated person can be stupid because education makes an intelligent person smarter, but a stupid person a bigger idiot.

Question: Is democracy a boon or bane?
Answer: Democracy means the rule of the people. Hence, the quality of governance in a democracy depends on the competency of the ruler, i.e. the people. In many ways, democracy is not much different from a dictatorship, as the majority of the people dictate the policies and vision of the government. While we can hope that an evil dictator will eventually die or be killed and replaced by a good dictator, we can never hope for the whole popular to perish and be replaced by enlightening people to choose a good leader. Hence, democracy sometimes looks hopeless since these countries are trapped in a vicious cycle of bad-people-bad-leaders. Hence, great transformations are unlikely in these countries, as bad people elect bad leaders, who in turn provide hopeless governance. Hence, democracy is often called the ‘tyranny of the majority’. Many countries like Singapore, China, and Russia have achieved excellent growth without proper democracy. Singapore has become one of the most developed countries in the world due to Lee Kuan Yu's leadership. on the other hand, Hitler was a democratically elected popular leader of Germany, who not only destroyed Germany but also caused unprecedented destruction of wealth and human life in the Second World War. It is a fact that today, most of the developed countries in the world are democracies because people are electing better people into power. Unfortunately, it is also a fact that many developing and poor countries are also democracies since people elect the worst people into power. Thus, democracy can be a boon or a bane, depending on the quality of the nation's people. Source of pictures: Google Images

Question: Why do government employees get corrupted easily?
Answer: The former Chief Vigilance Commissioner, Mr N Vittal, gave the most fitting reason to explain corruption in India by calling it a ''low-risk-high-profit-business”. The CVC made this statement in the year 2000 when India was ranked at 73rd position in the corruption perception index published by Transparency International. He hoped to bring the country to the 40th position. [1] Mr Vittal died last year in 2023. Unfortunately, contrary to his hope to reduce corruption in India and reach at least the 40th position within his tenure, India has been constantly declining in the anti-corruption ranking and now, after a quarter of a century, ranks 93 out of 180 countries. [2] The selection procedure for government employees is remarkably transparent and merit-based (within each category). By and large, agencies like UPSC, PSC or SSC responsible for the selection of government employees have been honest and even today, an Indian youth can hope to get the top job in government purely on merit, without paying any bribe or using influence. However, it is unfortunate that within a short time, most government officers get corrupted after joining the job because, as the CVC said, corruption is a high-profit-low-risk business in India. The laws against corruption are very strong in India, and if one gets caught taking even a Rs 1 bribe, he will go to jail and lose his job. However, in reality, not only do government officers make tons of money illegally, but their chances of getting caught in the act of corruption are very low. The tendency of government officials to become corrupt is based on the following cost-benefit analysis. Cost of Corruption Benefit of Corruption 1: Huge payout: A corrupt official can make more money in a single deal than an honest official can make in a lifetime. Who can forget the recovery of money in connection with the ED investigation against the IAS officer Pooja Singhal?[3] 2: Powerful Postings Imagine you are an IAS officer who never got a district posting but always got posted in secondary postings. In many positions, you are nothing more than a glorified clerk getting a decent salary. While corrupt officers get important positions in the government, honesty is sidelined and transferred frequently.[4] 3: Smoother Life: When most department officials are corrupt, trying to lead an honest life goes against the wind. While honest officials face frequent transfers and sideline postings, the corrupt rule the roost in government. Most people find that, after joining the government, corruption is better on a cost-benefit analysis because it is a low-risk, high-profit business. Unfortunately, as discussed above, corruption in India is constantly increasing compared to other nations because people elect corrupt, criminal, casteist and communal politicians in power, who in turn protect the corrupt and encourage corruption in every walk of life. Only a person with very high moral standards can protect himself from the virus of corruption in government, which has infected almost every branch of governance and eaten the nation like termites. The best way to eliminate corruption in India is to make corruption a High-Risk-Low-Profit job, However, all that will be possible only when people elect honest and competent politicians to power who will make such laws and create the right environment to root out corruption from India, Source of pictures: Google Images

Question: What is the meaning of "live your life to the fullest"? There are various stages of life like studentship, job, etc. So what is meaning of it at different stages?
Answer: Life is what you make it. We all go through different stages of life, each with its own set of challenges. The challenges of life are present in every stage, often bogging us down and preventing us from enjoying life to the fullest. It is human nature to seek pleasure and avoid pain. Unfortunately, the saying no-pain-no-gain is very much true in the world. There are no free lunches in the world, and to get anything in life, you must willingly pay the right price for it. Hence, to get pleasure, you have to suffer pain first. Since most people don’t like to suffer any type of pain in life, they also fail to acquire lasting joy. The greatest secret of life is that pain becomes a pleasure with practice, while pleasure becomes a pain with excessive engagement. Hence, We can live our lives to the fullest only when we understand the challenges, fulfil our responsibilities at every stage, accomplish our goals efficiently, and plan for the next stage of life. Elizabeth Streb sums this up, “When I’m taking my last breath, I want to look at how I used up the best of myself. How much did I sweat, push, pull, rip, fall, hit, crash, explode? My dream is to be so well-used that in my last half second, I just burst into dust.” Exactly my wish too. Source of picture: Google Images

Name: Awdhesh Singh
Question: Why are there so few Nobel laureates from India?
Answer: Let me share a funny story I received on one of my WhatsApp groups for the nth number of times. The story has been going viral for a few years because it contains some bitter truths about our society and perhaps the answer to this question. One day, a Colonel Sa'ab from the Army fell into a well. The soldiers would throw a rope into the well and pull Colonel Sa'ab out. The moment the Colonel would come up, the soldiers would leave the rope snap to attention and salute. The Colonel Sa'ab would fall back into the well. This happened many times. Someone suggested that a Brigadier be requested for help, because HE wouldn't have to salute the Colonel. So one Brigadier Sa'ab arrived. He threw the rope into the well, and Colonel Sa'ab grabbed it. The Brigadier Sa'ab began pulling the rope. As soon as Colonel Sa'ab reached the top of the well, he spotted Brigadier Sa'ab. He immediately left the rope and saluted. And he fell back once more, into the well. There was total silence. Then, everyone heard the desperate Colonel Sa'ab's voice from down below. "You idiots - get hold of a batchmate !!" The story contains the bitter truth about Indian society, where everyone is either below or high as compared to everyone else. Unfortunately, the hierarchy is considered so important that people would follow them, even if it can lead to the loss of life for someone. To win the Nobel Prize, you must be innovative and creative, which requires a free-thinking mind. This is impossible if you can’t eliminate the shackles of hierarchy. In Indian society, one's place is fixed due to one's birth, and whatever one does for the rest of one's life, it is almost impossible to change one's place in society. How can one get the motivation to think freely and create new things in life, when all your efforts are not going to make any difference in your position in society, or organisation? The chain of hierarchy starts at birth when your place is decided on the basis of your caste. Similarly, all professions, all institutes and colleges too are arranged in a nice heirarchy. The only difference is that your position in the government is decided on the day you are born in the government service, i.e. you are selected for the job. For the rest of your life, your position, even within the same batch, is fixed depending on the rank you achieved in the competitive examination. In the real world, intelligence, knowledge and wisdom is not a captive of birth, caste, or religion. Similarly, you don’t grow wiser and more knowledgeable with age. In the real world, most people become senile due to old age rather than becoming more creative, innovative and wiser. Worldwide, the greatest innovations have come from younger minds. In India, on the other hand, we value seniority and age as the most important criteria for judging the value of a person or his/her knowledge. So, even in the 21st century, most Indians believe that our ancestors created the best knowledge in every field, including philosophy, science, medicine, and health, which we must not question or even test for validity. We are thus living under illusions since none, but we find the old knowledge infallible or even true. How can innovation flourish in a country which worships the dead and torment the living? How can innovation take place in a country that believes the present generation can never be smarter than the previous generation? If India is to become a modern nation, it must stop glorifying the past, worship the old, and abolish the iron-clad hierarchy that has been gripping society for ages. Instead, we have to inculcate in the new generation a sense of belief and confidence that they are the smartest, next to none in the world, whether in the present or in the past. It reminds me of American entrepreneur Henry Ford's wise words: “Whether you think you can, or you think you can't--you're right.” Let us first think that we are the best; only then can we create the best and win not only the Nobel Prize, but achieve excellence in every field of life. Source of picture: Google Images

Name: Awdhesh Singh
Question: What is a controversial thing you believe in that you think shouldn't be controversial?
Answer: A few months ago, I got news from my father that one of my distant uncles, aged 82, died, probably due to cardiac arrest. He was quite healthy for his age. In the evening, he went to the village market, where he had tea samosas and a long chit-chat with his friends. Then he came home, had dinner, and slept as usual. However, when his wife checked up in the morning, he was no more. My father is 79 years old and lives in my native village with my mother, who is around 76 years old. The uncle was the closest friend of my father, and he was very heartbroken due to his sudden death. When I visited my village, everyone was discussing how good a man the uncle was and that he was blessed to have such a peaceful ending to his life. Soon, the matter of the death of my grandfather also came up, who died in 2016 at the age of 92. However, his ending was very painful as he lost his eyesight and his memory in the last few years. In the last two years of his life, he was bedridden. The two incidents made me think that medical science is so much developed today that it is possible for every single person to end his life peacefully, like a saint. The practice of ending the life of a patient to limit the patient's suffering is often called euthanasia. The patient in question would typically be terminally ill or experiencing great pain and suffering. In the case of euthanasia, the physician administers a fatal dose of a suitable drug to the patient to give him a peaceful death. However, euthanasia is a controversial topic and is illegal in most parts of the world, including India.[1] In 2018, an elderly couple from Thakurdwar wrote to the President's office, requesting permission for 'active euthanasia'. According to a report, the couple is satisfied with their life and no longer wishes to live.[2] They were never given any permission to end their life since no authority has the power to allow a person to end his life at will, which is illegal in India. Indian President can condone death sentence and give life to a person, but he has no power to allow a permit a person to end his life voluntarily. In my opinion, euthanasia must be legalised and even promoted to help people avoid suffering for themselves and their families and help them end their lives peacefully. While the right to life is provided in the Constitution as a fundamental right, the right to death should also be a constitutional right for every citizen.

Question: What is the BJP's role in addressing corruption in India?

Question: Why are people so enthusiastic about the UPSC exam when IAS, IRS, and IFS positions offer lower salaries compared to corporate jobs?
Answer: The first thing you notice when you join the services like IAS, IPS or IRS is the power and influence. You realise soon after joining the government in India that you are not a government servant, but actually the government itself. Most people erroneously think that politicians run the country and that government officers are just their puppets. The reality is that the government offices are empowered through the laws passed by the Parliament, which is superior to even the Prime Minister. Politicians can transfer them, but they can never exercise their powers, nor can they appoint or remove an IAS officer. They also have no role in their promotions, which is done by Departmental Promotion Commitee consisting of senior officers or UPSC Members. A government officer doesn’t have to seek permission from any politicians to take action in accordance with the law. For instance, as an IRS officer, on my first posting as an Assistant Commissioner, I had the power to issue a search warrant, order the seizure of goods, and even arrest a person who has evaded taxes beyond a certain amount. While over a period of time, the permission or approval of senior officers may be necessary for search and arrest, you still only have to approach your senior for permission (and not a politician), who is bound to give you permission if you have a solid case against the person. If you are acting according to the law and doing your duties honestly, your senior officers or politicians can’t do anything to you except transfer you to another charge, where you don’t lose even Rs 1 as salary. I had been an IRS officer for over 25 years and must have handled hundreds of cases, conducted over 500 searches, and arrested several dozen people, all using the legitimate powers vested in me by the law. Not once did I seek permission from any politician. If the powers were vested in me, I did not even have to inform the senior officers about the cases booked by us. (Picture above: Ajay Devgan as an IRS officer in the movie ‘Raid’, based on a real-life case[1]) When you work in corporate, you are just an employee getting paid for your work. You hardly exercise any authority over people who are not directly working under you. Moreover, you always fear that if the boss or the company is unhappy with you, they will remove you from the company immediately. So, if they want to work 12 hours a day, even work on weekends, you have no option, but to obey them, else you lose your job. On the contrary, in a government, even the Prime Minister can’t remove a peon unless the peon has done something illegal which necessitates his removal as per the law. Even if a corporate employee earns crores, he has no power or influence, while a lowly government officer has tremendous power and influence within his jurisdiction. Of course, with great power comes great responsibility. If you misuse your power, you may face punishment, including arrest and dismissal from service. You also tend to make personal enemies when you discharge your duties as IAS, IPS or IRS officers. However, if you are willing to pay the price, there is still no substitute for these services. Corporations can offer excellent pay and a cosy environment, but no corporation can ever offer you what you get in these services. I know most people working in corporations may disagree with my views, and some would claim that people join the government only for a bribe, but the fact remains that government jobs in India offer very decent salaries, great perks, job security, power, and influence, which no other service can offer, and it is an excellent choice even for a person who desires to remain honest all through his life. Hence, it is unsurprising that many people quit top-paying corporate jobs to join civil services.

Question: How can we make politicians tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth?

[1] You can easily imagine the fate of my batchmate and his family today. Unfortunately, this is exactly how the Indians treat educated and honest politicians. Mr Arvind Kejriwal, an ex-IRS and IITian, also came into Indian politics to clean it. However, we know the means he had to adopt to win elections. In fact, he followed such dubious means to win elections that today, almost all the top leaders of AAP are in jail, including Kejriwal, and none but his blind supporters would consider him honest. So, the dream of honest politicians in India can never be realised unless the people themselves become honest. If people remain corrupt, casteist, communal, and uneducated, we will get politicians of similar kind because in a democracy, as are the subjects (voters), so are the kings (politicians).

Question: Should the BJP consider Nitin Gadkari as the next PM?
Answer: After the 2024 Parliamentary elections of India, where the ruling party, BJP, failed to reach the majority of its own and could get only 241/542 seats, many of my friends, in their casual discussion, said that now Modi must step down and let Mr Gadkari become the next Prime Minister. I have great regard for Mr Nitin Gadkari, who, as a Minister for Road Transport & Highways in the Government of India, is doing an excellent job of developing national highways. He is perhaps the best-performing minister in the present Modi government. Further, Mr Gadkari seems like a good man who is always pleasant in his behaviour before the media, follows soft Hindutva, never speaks ill about others, talks business and works professionally. I also feel that he is far more acceptable to all political parties, including opposition parties, as compared to Mr Modi, who is seen as aggressive, arrogant, and a hardliner Hindu leader. However, to become the Prime Minister of India, you must also have legitimacy to govern the nation. If the election had been fought without the PM's face (like with Congress or the Indian alliance), then any alliance leader would have been acceptable to the people. For example, in 2004, Dr Manmohan Singh was made the PM, after the UPA alliance won, since no one was projected as the PM candidate. However, in the 2024 elections, the people did not vote for the BJP as a party but for Modi as its leader. If Modi had not been the leader or the face of the BJP, perhaps BJP would not have got even a fraction of the seats it got. The power of the PM does not flow from the chair of the PM, which was occupied earlier by non-leaders like I K Gujral, Deve Gowda, and Dr Manmohan Singh, but from the people's mandate. Without the people's support, a PM would be totally powerless since he wouldn’t be able to select or remove his ministers or frame the policy according to his vision. Hence, (good or bad) Modi is the only legitimate leader of the BJP who deserves to be the PM of India. If BJP/NDA instead chose Mr Nitin Gadgari as the next PM, he would be powerless in the absence of popular public support. Moreover, it would violate the people’s mandate, as they have voted for Modi to become the PM of India. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: What do you think the BJP got betrayed in UP?
Answer: Since 1990, after Mandal Commission, the UP politics revolved around caste lines, Dalits, OBC and General. Prior to 2014, the state was dominated by two parties, In 2014, the BJP surprised everyone by successfully using the Hindutva politics in UP, fielding the Gujarat CM Modi in Varanasi. Somehow, most Hindus voted for BJP in 2014, 2017, 2019 and 2022 on the religious plank, and they won the election by a handsome margin. However, UP continue to be a casteist society, where the caste identity of people matters a lot. Further, Yogi Adityanath is not considered to be fair to all Hindus, and many people found him favouring his own caste, Kshatriya/Thakur. This led to the alienation of other castes from the BJP. The BJP tried to balance the caste calculus by denying some prominent Thankur leaders tickets, which, instead of benefiting the BJP, ended up alienating even Thakurs from the party. On the other side, in the 2024 election, the SP and Congress successfully played the caste card by promising a caste census and giving proportionate reservations on the basis of caste. In addition, they also promised lots of freebies to the voters. Hence, the move of the INDIA alliance revived caste politics again, and the BJP failed to win seats even in Ayodhya and lost badly in Amethi and Sultanpur. Even Mr Modi's margin of victory reduced substantially in 2024 to just around 1.5 lakhs, which was 1/3rd of the victory margin of 2019, while Rahul Gandhi won from Raiberely with nearly 4 lakh votes, increasing the victory margin 2.5 times.[1] So, BJP lost UP not due to betrayal of the UP voters but because of the caste politics well played by SP and Congress. BJP paid the price of not taking into account the caste sensibilities in UP and hoping that all Hindus will be united behind them due to Ram Mandir.

Question: When something bad happens after someone has done something seen as 'bad', why do people say this is an example of karma?
Answer: Karma is not a scientific principle but a matter of faith. According to the principle of karma (action), The karma principle is a good theory as it motivates people to do good things for society like honesty, love, compassion, and duty) and shun doing actions that are bad for society. The Karma principle works quite well in fiction, movies, and mythologies, where the good characters always win in the end, and the evil characters always lose. However, in practically every real-world arena (politics, bureaucracy, business, film), good people (honest, loving, kind, law-abiding) usually lose. In contrast, bad people (corrupt, criminal, cruel, heartless) frequently win in almost every field of life. In fact, the victory of evil people has become so common that it rarely makes news in the world. As they say in journalism, “If a dog bites a man (which is very common), it is not a news. But if a man bites a dog (which rarely happens), it is news.”[1] Hence, it is not surprising tht when once in a while, bad people suffer bad consequences (which rarely happens), it becomes a news. Such type of exceptional occurrences make good people happy as their faith is validated through such news. Hence, the faithful people rejoice that there is a God who punishes the bad people for their evil karma, which gives them some hope that their good karma will bring them good fruits in the future.

Question: What is your opinion on the saying 'If you love someone, set them free'?
Answer: If you love someone, the person becomes a part of you emotionally because their happiness and sorrow become your own. While you may not be concerned so much about hundreds of people dying in a remote part of the world, you are concerned if your loved one is hurt even a bit. In the same way, if your loved ones achieve success in life or are happy, you feel successful and happy for them. If you love someone, not only does their joy and sorrow become your own, but you also feel responsible for their joy and sorrow. Hence, it is your duty to act in the best interest of your loved ones, and this may sometimes mean disciplining them if they are going down the wrong path or doing something that will harm them. Let us take some examples. There is a valuable lesson in the following Aesops’ Fable. A boy stole a lesson book from one of his schoolfellows and took it home to his Mother. She abstained from beating him. The next time, he stole a cloak and brought it to her, and she again commended him. The youth advanced to adulthood and stole things of still greater value. At last, he was caught in the very act and, having his hands bound behind him, was led away to the place of public execution. His Mother followed in the crowd and violently beat her breast in sorrow, whereupon the young man said, "I wish to say something to my Mother in her ear." She came close to him, and he quickly seized her ear with his teeth and bit it off. The Mother upbraided him as an unnatural child, whereon he replied, "Ah! if you had beaten me when I first stole and brought to you that lesson book, I should not have come to this, nor have been thus led to a disgraceful death."[1] There can be serious consequences for freeing your loved ones. In India, recently, a 17-year-old boy in an intoxicated condition was illegally driving a Porsche car, killing two people on the road. Later on, parents tried to protect their child, and after an investigation, the whole family of the child and doctors giving false reports were arrested.[2] The following message is going viral on WhatsApp about this incident. The 17 years old minor in Pune.. - Destroyed a 2 Crore Porsche. - Life of 2 young professionals - Destroyed 2 families of victims - His father is in Jail. - His Grandfather is in Jail - His Mother was also arrested. - Took away Job of 3 Doctors - Took away Job of 2 Policeman - The boy will be jailed for long Morale of the story: Raise your children well All this happened because the child's parents followed the philosophy of setting their loved one free. Perhaps, when their child started making smaller mischief, instead of stopping the child or punishing the child, they protected the child, and now the child's life is spoiled forever. It is our duty to constantly observe our loved ones because we are concerned about their happiness and sorrow. We must also try to help and guide them as much as we can to make their life happier. However, your ultimate goal must be to gradually free them by making them more able, disciplined, and wise so that they can take care of themselves and follow the right path without your help and support. Question: Does repeating a lie over and over make it the truth?
Answer: Unfortunately, a lie indeed becomes a truth if it is repeated over and over again. Interestingly, no human being can accept a lie knowingly. However, if a set of interconnected lies is spread smartly, it is possible to convince people that the lie is true and transform it into the truth. Take, for instance, the following Joke, which went viral some years ago. I told my son, “You will marry the girl I choose.” He said, “NO!” I told him, “She is Bill Gates’ daughter.” He said, “OK.” I called Bill Gates and said, “I want your daughter to marry my son.” Bill Gates said, “NO.” I told Bill Gates, My son is the CEO of the World Bank.” Bill Gates said, “OK.” I called the President of the World Bank and asked him to make my son the CEO. He said, “NO.” I told him, “My son is Bill Gates’ son-in-law.” He said, “OK.”[1] As you can see from the above story, a series of interconnected lies actually became the truth because they were all spoken with intelligence, keeping the psychology of the listeners in mind. While the above story seems hypothetical, many lies are indeed accepted today as truth. Let me give you some examples. There is no evidence whatsoever of God, and yet billions of people around the world believe in the existence of God, thanks to the mythologies, Scriptures, temples, rituals, priests, punishment for heresy, politicians and kings who made people believe in God. Tell these religious people that God does not exist, and they will become your enemy number one. When the media repeatedly lies by projecting a particular leader as great, promoting the leader's positive traits due to vested interest, fear, or temptation, and suppressing all the leader's negative traits, gradually, the leader becomes indeed the most popular leader among the people. For instance, these leaders were the most popular leaders in their country at their time, thanks to the lies spread by them to fool the masses. Likewise, when people falsely start projecting a person as a fool, corrupt, inefficient, or ignorant and criticising a good person, gradually, the people start believing so, and the person indeed starts behaving strangely and foolishly. Many good people, like Jesus Christ and Socrates, were perceived as evil at their time, thanks to the repeated lies told about them. Most people don’t have the ability to identify the truth through critical thinking and self-investigation. As a result, they lap up any lie as truth if it is popular and suits them. Question: If you had to change one thing you did in the past, what would it be and why did you pick it?
Answer: That is a very interesting question. I usually don’t think about changing my past because it is simply impossible. But assuming I can do it, let me try to answer this question. When I was in class 12th (1983), I had no idea of the IIT-JEE examination, as no one in my family was an engineer. However, I had a friend named Alok Mathur, whose father was a Gold Medalist from Roorkee University (now IIT-Roorkee), and his two elder brothers were in IIT Kanpur. He joined postal coaching of Agrawal Classes and suggested to me that I should share the course and the fee (which was Rs 600 then, so I had to pay Rs 300 to share the course). In those days, I was against the idea of coaching, so I refused. The result was that though we used to score similar marks in school, he got into IIT Kanpur with a 322 rank, while I got IT-BHU Varanasi with a 1331 rank. So, perhaps I should have accepted his advice and joined Agrawal Classes. On second thought, I feel that I should not have gone to IIT or done Mechanical Engineering at all because, after four years, I was going to write UPSC civil services. Please permit me to change my action once. My optionals for civil services were mathematics and physics, which I had to study from scratch, and I wasted my four years studying mechanical engineering. How good it would have been if I had instead chosen BSc course followed by M Sc, and spent four years studying Mathematics and Physics. I am sure that if I had done B Sc, I would have got the top rank in the civil services examination and perhaps been selected for IAS with the top rank, and got home cadre. But then, what was the use of becoming an IAS if, after a decade, I was to do the PhD, and quit the civil services to become a writer? I would have quit IAS anyway. So, it seems that I wasted 25 years of my life in civil services, and today, I am not using anything I learned in civil services. Please permit me to change the ‘one thing’ once again. I should have joined PhD after my M Tech and become a professor in some prestigious college. Perhaps I would have published thousands of research papers and written dozens of books by now. However, all my books would have been on technical subjects, which would have been read by a few thousand people. That would have been worse than what I am doing today. I think I have to change my one thing once again. Oh! I am so confused. I accept that I have not made the best decisions in my life. However, if I had made better decisions (from today’s perspective), as I discussed above, I would have perhaps missed many things in life, like: Hence, finally, I decided not to change anything I did in the past because everything I have done in my life has given me unique and beautiful experiences, and added lustre to my life. What I am today is due to the experiences of my life. If I change anything of the past, I will no longer be the same person as I am now. Since I love my life today and enjoy every moment of my life, I would not like to opt for a different life by changing anything that I did in the past.

Question: What is the biggest life lesson you have ever learned?
Answer: Let me share with you the greatest lesson I have learned in life. We all enjoy jokes and funny stories, as in every story, there is someone so stupid, and we laugh at his foolishness. Take, for instance, this joke, which has many versions available on the internet. An American lawyer and a Nigerian are sitting next to each other on a long flight. The lawyer believes that Nigerians are so dumb that he could put something over on them easily, So the lawyer asks if the Nigerian would like to play a fun game. The Nigerian is tired and just wants to take a nap, so he politely declines and tries to catch a few winks. The American lawyer persists, and says that the game is a lot of fun. I ask you a question, and if you don't know the answer, you pay me only $5; you ask me one, and if I don't know the answer, I will pay you $500, he says. This catches the Nigerian's attention, and to keep the lawyer quiet, he agrees to play the game. The lawyer asks the first question. 'What's the distance from The Earth to the Moon?' The Nigerian doesn't say a word, reaches in his pocket pulls out a five-dollar bill, and hands it to the lawyer. Now, it's the Nigerian's turn. He asks the lawyer, 'What goes up a hill with three legs, and comes down with four?' The lawyer uses his laptop and searches all references he could find on the Net. He sends e-mails to all the smart friends he knows, all to no avail. After one hour of searching he finally gives up. He wakes up the Nigerian and hands him $500. The Nigerian pockets the $500 and goes right back to sleep. The lawyer is going nuts, not knowing the answer. He wakes the Nigerian up and asks, 'Well, so what goes up a hill with three legs and comes down with four?' The Nigerian reaches in his pocket, hands the lawyer $5 and goes back to sleep.[1] We usually laugh at such jokes. However, there is a deep wisdom hidden in this story. And the wisdom is, “If there is no solution to a problem, it is not a problem.” For instance, illness is a problem because there is a solution to illness. However, death or old age is not a problem since there is no way any person can avoid death or illness. Now, if we waste our time thinking about old age and death, we will get nothing in return and spoil our lives. Likewise, there are many problems where people waste lots of time without finding a solution. For instance, in India, many people are bothered too much about caste-based reservations, which legally discriminate against people on a caste basis. However, if you have some wisdom, you know that reservation is never going to go away because democracy is the dictatorship of the majority. Almost 90% of Indians benefit from one or other form of reservation. Similarly, many people are concerned about the criminal, corrupt, casteist and communal politicians getting elected into power while the honest people are voted out. If you have any wisdom, you know that politicians represent the people they lead, and so are the people, and so are the politicians in the country. Hence, unless you wish to join politics to bring fundamental change in society by transforming the view of the people, there is no point in cribbing about something inevitable. Hence, next time you are bothered too much about an issue, think if there is a solution to the problem. If no solution exists, stop treating that as a problem and instead focus your attention on such issues where you can find a solution, individually or collectively. It may be wise to remember the wisdom of the following serenity prayer. Also, the next time you read a joke, apply your mind to discover the wisdom in it. Our world is not straight, and we often need jokes to tell the deepest truth about life. Source of Image: Google Images

Question: Is it bad to give unsolicited advice? Why?
Answer: Advice is like a medicine, which should normally be given when the patient demands it. However, if your loved one, a family member or a friend gets sick and refuses to acknowledge his illness, will you not advise the person to go to a doctor and take medicine? While it may be a bad idea to give unsolicited advice to a stranger, it is necessary that we must give advice to the people who are close to us, or whom we love, whether or not they seek our advice, and they will thank you for your unsolicited advice. Around 2006, many IRS officers resigned from the service to join private sector jobs. In those days, government salaries were pathetic. I was an Additional Commission with 16 years of seniority, yet my salary was around Rs 35,000 pm (CTC around Rs 5 lakhs per annum). Almost all the IRS officers who resigned joined BIG 4 (Deloitte, EY, KPMG, and PwC) and were offered salaries ranging from Rs 20–50 lakhs per annum plus bonuses. I, too, was thinking of quitting the service. However, in an official meeting, when this issue was discussed, and I expressed my desire to quit the job, one of my seniors (whom I will call PK) told me bluntly, “Awdhesh! How long will you live for your career? Your daughter is in class 8th and 9th; they need your time and help. If you join a private company, you may get money, but you will have no time for your children. At this stage of your life, you must give your time to your children and help them make a good career for themselves.” Somehow, I got so much influenced by his advice that I decided to give up the idea of changing my job, and started teaching my children every day after office hours, which not only helped me build a strong relationship with my children but also helped them perform quite well in their senior classes, get selected in good Engineering colleges and build a good career for themselves. Even today, I feel extremely grateful for PK for his advice. Almost a decade later, when I was posted in Chennai, Mr PK came to my home, and we had dinner. I reminded him of his advice and told him how thankful I was for his advice. Interestingly, he did not even remember giving me such advice. In the Bible, Jesus tells of a farmer who sows seed indiscriminately. Some seed falls on the path (wayside) with no soil, some on rocky ground with little soil, some on soil which contains thorns, and some on good soil. In the first case, the seed is taken away; in the second and third soils, the seed fails to produce a crop; but when it falls on good soil, it grows and yields thirty-, sixty-, or a hundred-fold.”[1] Just like a seed may provide a good yield when sown on good soil, sound advice can change a person's life forever. It was unsolicited advice given by a few saints that transformed Valmiki from a bandit to a Maharshi (great saint). [2] Hence, it is not always wrong to give unsolicited advice. Most people are hesitant to seek advice due to self-respect or ego, even when they are in trouble and unable to find a way to get out of it. If you give the right advice to such a person in the right manner, you can help the person overcome his problems and lead a good life, thus improving society and the world. Question: What is the most respected service in India (IAS, IPS, or IRS) and why?
Answer: Frankly, I don’t know if any of the government officers are respected nowadays. Most urban and educated people actually hate government officers and consider them corrupt, inefficient, and puppets of politicians. However, nearly everyone fears government officers due to their power and doesn’t want to mess with them. It is always beneficial to know the senior government officers in India who can help them in their time of need. In a developing country like India, government officers play an important role in development as they collect tax revenue, maintain law and order, create and maintain infrastructure, provide education and healthcare to the common people, and implement the poor's development and poverty alleviation schemes. The officers are respected when they perform their duties well and serve the nation. Hence, the respect for a service depends on the number of people it serves and its contribution to national development. The order of respect for India's three services, IAS, IPS, and IRS, is as follows. 1: Indian Administrative Service (IAS) IAS is certainly the most powerful and respected service in India. IAS officers occupy the top position in a district as District Magistrates or Collectors and supervise the work of almost all state government departments. (Anudeep Durishetty, IAS, Kothagudem Collector) [1] When they get promoted, they become secretaries in the ministries and contribute to the policy-making and supervision of all state and central government departments. 2: Indian Police Service (IPS) IPS officers head all the police departments in India. They are responsible for maintaining law and order, collecting intelligence, and investigating all types of criminal cases. They enjoy maximum power as Superintendent of Police (SP) or Commission in a district/city. (Picture above: Sanjay Arora, IPS, the new Commissioner of Delhi Police)[2] The police department is the most powerful department in India, but it is not known for its professionalism and integrity. Hence, IPS officers, though very powerful, do not enjoy as much respect from the common people as they are feared. 3: Indian Revenue Service (IRS) The IRS is a central government service that works under the Ministry of Finance of India. It is the most powerful department of the central government, as it is the only agency that deals with the common people and has jurisdiction over all of India. IRS officers collect the central government's taxes and head agencies like the Enforcement Directorate, which deals with financial crimes and money laundering. (Mr P.B. Sekaran, IRS, the Principal Chief Commissioner of Income Tax)[3] Due to high tax threshold limits, automation and liberalisation, IRS officers are little known to the common people in rural and semi-urban areas, as most people have to never deal with the tax department. However, they are well known to businessmen and the well-off section of society, which pays taxes to the government. The IRS officers work more professionally among all services and face the least interference. They also enjoy the highest respect and power among the central government department but are not as well known to the common people as IAS and IPS.

Question: Why do even highly educated people believe in God even though there is no strong evidence of his/her existence?
Answer: Suppose you are addicted to smoking, and you are also an educated person who knows that cigarette smoking is injurious to your health and may cause cancer. For instance, you are aware of the study that people who smoke one packet of cigarettes a day may develop as many as 150 extra mutations in their lungs every year, which can eventually lead to cancer. You are fully aware that tobacco smoking claims the lives of at least six million people every year, and if current trends continue, the World Health Organisation predicts more than 1 billion tobacco-related deaths in this century.[1] Suppose you know the harmful effects of smoking and still smoke every day. In that case, you face cognitive dissonance, which is defined as the mental discomfort or psychological stress of performing an action that contradicts personal beliefs, ideals and values. Cognitive dissonance causes continuous mental stress, and you lose your peace of mind. Hence, you desperately want to reduce dissonance to maximise happiness and minimize pain. Cognitive dissonance can be reduced by If you exercise the first alternative, you quit smoking so that your thoughts/beliefs (smoking is harmful to health) and actions (no smoking) align with each other. However, it is difficult to get rid of any addiction. Hence, most people find it difficult to follow the second option. Instead of quitting smoking, they stop reading such studies and instead convince themselves that smoking does not cause much harm, often by referring to the example of those people who smoke regularly but live long and also quoting the nonsmokers who died young. For instance, when a well-known comedy superstar, Groucho Marx, became disturbed by the effects of smoking, after reading an article on the subject, he gave up reading. [2] Religion is far more addictive than smoking. No wonder Karl Marx called religion the OPIUM of the masses. Interestingly, while the law prohibits smoking till you become an adult, the dose of religion is given to a child from a very early age. Hence, by the time a human being becomes an adult, he/she has already become a religious addict, if brought up in a religious family. When that addicted person acquires higher education, he learns the fallacies of religion and questions his belief in God. He thus faces cognitive dissonance because Hence, an educated and rational person loses peace of mind due to cognitive dissonance, i.e. conflict between his thoughts and actions, and he desperately wishes to resolve the dissonance to get the peace of mind. There are two methods to resolve cognitive dissonance, which is caused by false belief in God and religion. The first option is tough to follow because breaking a habit that has been inculcated since childhood is challenging. Moreover, even if you are a highly determined person, you don’t want to become socially ostracised by your friends, family and society, who all believe in God and have deep faith in their religion. Hence, most people choose the second option by continuing with all religious activities. As long as you keep praying, following religious rituals, and visiting temples and pilgrimages, even if it is to gain the goodwill of society, your mind is forced to justify your actions, which is only possible if you believe in God. Hence, however educated you become, you can’t stop believing in God unless you align your actions with your beliefs and develop the courage to discard all religious activities, which is not only difficult but almost impossible for most people in the world.

Question: What is the reason behind many Indians being hesitant to ask questions? How can this fear be overcome and encourage them to ask questions?
Answer: After being selected for the IRS, my first posting was in a Central Excise Division. As a young officer, I did lots of things in the division, like renovating the office, installing computers, etc. I also booked a number of cases, some of them involved a noble modus operenti. After a couple of months, the Member Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBIC) visited the place. My Joint Commissioner (JC), who was quite fond of me and appreciated my initiative, requested the member to visit my division. Accordingly, the Member, with the Commissioner and other senior officers, made an unscheduled visit to my office and inspected my office. When the Member was having tea in my office, he casually asked me to discuss some recent cases. I had then booked an excellent case involving a huge amount of revenue and had all India ramifications. I enthusiastically started explaining the case to the member. However, the Member had little patience. He immediately told me that I had no case. He must have wondered, ‘How can a young officer with less than six months of experience make a case that they could not think of?’ However, I was prepared well and told him about the legal points, case laws, etc. The Member had no answer to my questions. He got irritated and said, “Do you want a solution or want to create a problem?” My JC was sitting next to me. He pressed my hand, signalling me to keep quiet. I submitted to the member, “I want a solution.” He then gave his reasoning about the case, and I told him that I would surely look into the case afresh. My JC later told me, “Never argue with Member. If he becomes happy, he will call you to the Board (where you get no facility), and if he gets angry, he will post you to some God-forsaken place.” I booked the case anyway, but I learned a valuable lesson: I must avoid arguing with seniors. This is how the Indian mind works. If you are a senior, older, or have a higher degree, you automatically become superior to those who are junior, younger or have lesser qualifications. India is a highly hierarchical society, and its impact is visible in every single institution. The worst thing is that you can never change your position in the hierarchy, no matter how good, competent, or hardworking you may be. Due to rigid hierarchy, you achieve your high position without merit. Hence, if someone junior questions you, he is indirectly challenging your authority, for which the person needs to be punished. Our training starts at a younger age, when we are told that we should not question our teachers because their status is even above God. Sant Kabir said this in the following Doha, "Guru Govind dou khade, kaake laagoon paye Balihari guru aapki, Govind diyo milaye." Translation I face both God and my guru. Whom should I bow to first? I first bow to my guru because he's the one who showed me the path to God.[1] We don’t question our philosophies like that of Gita or Buddha because older is always superior to younger. While humans around the world are getting smarter with time, Indians are getting so dumb that they can not even match the wisdom and knowledge acquired by their ancestors thousands of years ago. Most Indians still believe that Vedas, Upanishads and Puranas written several thousand years ago have all the wisdom of the world, including the scientific knowledge, without even reading them. India may be the only society in the world that considers its mythologies History. Even today, the entire politics revolves around mythologies, which everyone must accept as true without seeking any proof or validation. If you ask questions, you are called sickular, anti-national, anti-religion, traitor etc., and ridiculed. In such an environment, how can one ask questions? However, unless we ask questions, we can’t grow as a person, and India can’t grow as a nation. Karl Popper has wisely said, “The growth of knowledge depends entirely on disagreement”. You must overcome this fear yourself, travel on the path less travelled, and achieve success in life. Once you become successful, most Indians will make you their IDOL, follow you like a devotee, accept your wisdom as the words of God, and thus become wiser themselves. Question: Why do people find difficult to admit when they are wrong?
Answer: We may be wrong for two reasons. 1: Factual Mistakes The first type of mistake is related to facts. For instance, during a discussion, I made a claim that the rate of FD interest in India in 2016 was 9%, while my relative claimed that it was 7%. I decided to do some Google searches, and I found that he was right. I readily admitted my mistake. You don’t have any option in such a matter as the facts can be verified and remain the same for everyone. Most people would, therefore, admit their mistakes in factual matters. 2: Decisions Suppose you are doing a well-paid job, and you quit your job to prepare for the civil services examination in India or try to pursue your passion for writing, music or something else. Now, after spending a decade, you have failed to realise your dream, and your life is much worse. Similarly, you may invest your hard-earned money in some stock or property, and the prices crash after a few years, and you lose lots of money. Likewise, suppose you find your love and get married to the person. However, after a few years, you realise that you have no compatibility with the person, and your life has become miserable after marriage. The decisions would be considered wrong in all the above cases as they did not lead to the desired consequences. However, such decisions are not wrong; they appear to be wrong due to hindsight bias. Hindsight bias involves the tendency to assume that people know the outcome of an event after the outcome has already been determined. It is an I-knew-it-all-along phenomenon that is a common tendency for people to perceive past events as having been more predictable than they were. We often judge other people wrong due to the hindsight bias, while justify our actions as we know the reasons for taking a particular decision. We all get wiser after the outcome is known and often imagine that we have known about it since the beginning. For instance, if a young person leaves a job to prepare for the civil services examination and fails, most people would claim that they already know that the person does not have the ability and talent to crack civil services. However, if the person succeeds, they would say that they knew all along that the person would get through. Should you blame yourself if you did not study those topics which came in the examination? [1] Clearly, you did not prepare for those topics because you were not sure they would be included in the examination. It was just a matter of chance that these questions came in the examination, which you thought, along with many other questions, as probable. It is only due to your hindsight bias that you now think that you know that those questions would come in the examination. Hence, if you make a well-thought-out decision and it goes wrong, you need not admit that your decision was wrong, even if the whole world believes so, due to their hindsight bias.

Question: Some people advice, "Give all your heart and work towards your passion, money will follow", while some say "First get a job and achieve financial freedom, then you can follow your passion". Which one is more advisable by you?
Answer: While serving as an IRS officer, I took study leave in 2002 to pursue my PhD from IIITM Gwalior. During my PhD, I published seven research papers in International Journals and Conferences and developed a passion for writing. In 2005, I wrote my first book ‘Change your Nature to Change Your Life” and sent it to almost a dozen publishers. However, all the publishers rejected by book, and as a result, this book was never published. However, I kept writing in different online forums and, by 2012, published around 500 articles on different forums. I wrote my next book, Practising Spiritual Intelligence, in 2012, which the Wisdom Tree published in 2013. The book was launched on 1st July 2013 by Mr Jay Panda, Honorable Member of Parliament in Delhi. My passion for writing was so overpowering that 2016, I quit IRS to become a full-time writer. As of now, after 20 years of following my passion, I have got NINE books published, which have been sold over 100,000 copies. I am also one of the top writers on Quora, with more than 350K followers and 250M views. Hence, I can consider myself a reasonably successful writer and would perhaps rank in the top 1% of writers in terms of royalties. Yet, despite all the success, my annual income from the royalty for my books is hardly Rs 25,000 ($300) pm. It is perhaps less than the minimum wages given to any skilled worker in India. There is no way I can survive with this small income and live a decent life. If I am living a decent life today, and able to follow my passion, it is because I worked in the IRS for 25 years, from where I get a handsome pension every month, My story is the story of almost all people who follow their passion. Unfortunately, most people know the stories of only those people who are in the top 0.01% and are making good money by following their passions. These people live lavish lifestyles, like the actor Nawazuddin Siddiqui, who, after years of struggle, lives in a luxurious bungalow in Mumbai.[1] Such successful people often advise people, "Give all your heart and work towards your passion, money will follow." However, they constitute a very small minuscule of people who make good money following their passion. The sad reality is that 99.99% of the people who follow their passion struggle to make a decent living following their passion. Their passion die a slow death due to nonfulfillment of basic needs like food, clothing and shelter. It is prudent not to be swayed by the anecdotal evidence but rather see the holistic picture. Hence, my advice is, "First, get a job and achieve financial freedom, then you can follow your passion". Of course, if you are a Starkid or belong to a well-off family and your parents can financially support you in following your passion, you don’t need to get a job for financial security, and you can follow your passion any time in your life.

Question: Despite the fact that we are moving forward in a new digital century, the process of selecting a UPSC aspirant for civil services remains the same. On that note, can we say that the selection procedure for the UPSC exam has outdated?
Answer: The civil services examination for the selection of the top bureaucrats in India started with the setting up of the Civil Service Commission in 1854 in London, and the competitive examinations were started in 1855[1]. It is indeed a wonder that the same selection process through UPSC continues for more than 170 years, and even after India gained independence from British rule, and the world has totally changed. However, not many people in India, particularly the civil servants and the aspirants, would agree that the system is outdated, as they can’t imagine a better system. The purpose of the UPSC civil services examination is to select the most suitable candidate for the top civil services in India, such as IAS, IPS, IFS, IRS, and more than a dozen other services, including many Group B services. Let us analyse UPSC's present selection procedure and understand whether it is the best or highly outdated system of selection. Let me start with the selection procedure for marriage in the olden days for a boy and a girl. In the past, boys and girls had no say in selecting their life partners, who were decided by their parents or the family's eldest member. However, even the parents were not free to select the boy and girl for their offspring. Typically, the proposal will come from the girl's side through an intermediary (Bicholia) after matching the Kundli (Horoscope), caste, Gotra, and economic status/dowry. The boy and girl would usually see each other on the wedding night, and the girl would wear a veil. However, the marriages would be for a lifetime, as there was no provision for divorce in the Hindu religion. So, even if you get married to the worst person or a totally incompatible person, you have to carry the relationship until the end of your life. However, India has changed a lot in the last 170 years, and today, boys and girls select each other and marry only if they are compatible with each other. Unfortunately, civil services in India still follow the old age practice, as evidenced by the following: If India is to become a developed country in the future, it must also have a modern system of governance like other developed countries. The government must select the best candidate for every job (instead of the one-comptition-fit-all method of UPSC), and the candidate must choose the job that suits their aptitude and temperament. It means that the hierarchy of services(like the caste system) has to go, and every service must be given the same prestige so that candidates choose the services according to their aptitude and not based on hierarchy. I hope that the Government of India seriously considers discarding this old system of selection and introducing a new system for selecting the top civil servants of India according to the needs of modern times. Question: What is the best way to choose life partner?
Answer: A human being may be said to have four principal components, i.e. physical, mental, emotional and spiritual. When you choose a person as a life partner, you must ensure the compatibility of all four components. 1: Physical Compatibility Your life partner must be physically compatible with you. It means that there must not be much difference between physical attractiveness, height, weight, age, etc., between the life partners. For instance, if one is ugly-looking while the other is very attractive, the relationship may not last long. Similarly, the age difference or height difference must also be reasonable. 2: Mental Compatibiltiy Imagine that you are a PhD while your spouse is illiterate! It is obvious that the match may not last long. It would be better if the intellectual level of the couples also matched because an ideal life partner must also be your good friend, which shall be possible only if their thoughts match, at least on most of the issues. 3: Emotional Compatibility Love is the strongest emotion known to humankind. The relationship will weaken if you don’t feel emotional attraction towards your partner. Emotions are based on chemistry, which is involuntary, unpredictable, but very powerful. The Indian poet Mirza Ghalib beautifully said, Ishq par zor nahin, hai yeh voh aatish Ghalib Ke lagaey na lagey aur bujhaey na bane English Translation Love is a flame on which you have no control, O Ghalib! You can neither lit the flame (of love), nor can you extinguish it at will. Hence, listen to your heart before choosing your partner. However, the feelings must be on both sides. One-sided love in a relationship is nothing less than a poison, which kills the love gradually and even transforms love into hatred. 4: Spiritual Compatibility "Love is composed of a single soul inhabiting two bodies," said the Greek philosopher Aristotle. How true! Love lasts longest when the souls of the beloved become one. Our souls contain our deepest values, conscience, and beliefs. Having common values is a must for a lasting relationship. The relationship between corrupt and honest, truthful and liar, faithful and unfaithful, religious and atheists, artists and materialists can’t last long. They choose to marry the person based on looks, education, or feelings, rather than checking their compatibility at all four levels. Question: Why do the rich get richer?
Answer: What happens when you throw a ball upward in the air? It will go up to a height and then fall back to earth again. So it is wisely said, “What goes up comes down”. However, in physics, there is an interesting concept of “escape velocity”, which is defined as “the minimum speed an object must reach to break free from the gravitational pull of a body without further propulsion.” In simple terms, if you throw a ball with the escape velocity, it will never come back to earth again. The escape velocity on Earth is measured to be 11.2 km/second.[1] Likewise, when you acquire a certain minimum amount of wealth, you not only become rich, but you will keep getting richer and richer and never become poor again, unless you fall into bad habits or gamble your money away. It is a fact that all over the world, the rich people are getting richer, while the poor are getting poorer relative to each other. According to the Oxfam report of 2023, It is evident that the gap between the rich and poor is increasing every year. If you become rich once, you keep getting richer due to the following reasons. Jesus Christ said this bitter truth of life more than two thousand years ago, “Whoever has will be given more, and they will have an abundance. Whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken from them.” Therefore, it is no wonder that almost everyone in the world wants to become rich. They know that once they become rich, they and future generations will escape from the millions of problems that poor people face every day.

Question: What's the worst thing that can happen to a person when preparing for the UPSC? Do some people really go crazy and end up in an asylum?
Answer: Can you believe that some people are so desperate about the civil services that they are willing to spend their entire lives preparing for them? I could not believe the desperation of some people when I read this news. Meet Pushpendra Shrivastava, the oldest government job aspirant in New Delhi’s Mukherjee Nagar, the heart of UPSC coaching institutes. In the last 27 years, Pushpendra has given 73 preliminary examinations, 43 Mains examinations, and 8 interviews for State and Union Public Service Commissions. He is already 47, and going on 48, but he isn’t done yet. Right now, he is busy preparing for the interview round for the Madhya Pradesh Public Service Commission. The cut-off age in Madhya Pradesh was 40 years, which the state government increased to 43 in 2022 following the COVID-19 pandemic while relaxing the age limit by five more years for reserved categories (EWS, SC, ST, OBC) and women. [1] So, you can take civil services examinations up to the age of 48 years in MP. Since it takes a minimum of one year for the whole process of selection to be completed, you can join up to 49 years, and then you will have only 11 years of service left till retirement. While I wish him all the best for his interview and selection, what would happen if he does not get selected in this attempt as well? I fear that he would get depressed and may end up in asylum. While I feel sorry for the people who spent all their youth and the best part of their lives preparing for the civil services examination, governments in India are no less responsible for the misery of the civil services aspirants. When I wrote the civil services examination in 1989, the maximum age was 26 for the general category, and only 3 attempts were allowed. In my opinion, that was a better system than what exists today. If you exhaust your attempts at 26 years and don’t get selected (which is bound to happen to 99.9% of the candidates due to a limited number of seats), you still have sufficient time to start fresh and make a good career for yourself. However, when you have grown up in your 30s and 40s preparing for civil services, and then fail to make it, your life is sure to get miserable as starting a new career would then be nearly impossible. After spending more than 25 years in civil services as an IRS officer and having close knowledge of other civil services, I can say that civil services is just another job with its pros and cons, and it certainly is not worth wasting your life for it. However, there are few takers of my advice. Instead, if Pushpendra get success, Bollywood will make a couple of movies on his life, like 12th Fail, to motivate Indian youths to never give up when writing civil services examination.

Question: If I easily trust everyone, would that be considered a strength or weakness?
Answer: Trust is like wealth, which has to be earned with a lifetime of effort. You become trustworthy when you always walk your talk and fulfil your promises. An intelligent person is one who only trusts trustworthy people. Hence, if you can easily trust everyone, it means that you are unable to judge their trustworthiness. If people learn that you blindly trust everyone, many will be ready to exploit your trust for their selfish benefit. If you trust a cunning and smart person, you may ruin your life and the lives of your loved ones. As a matter of fact, you must not trust ANY person absolutely, but always develop the habit of keep checking the trustworthiness of people from time to time. This is what we learn from the following Mahabharatha story. Dronacharya was the Guru and the commander-in-chief of the Kaurava army. Knowing it would be impossible to defeat an armed Drona, Krishna suggests a plan to disarm Drona by some means of contrivance. Accordingly, Bhima killed an elephant named Ashwatthama and then claimed to Drona that he had killed his son with the same name. Disbelieving his claim, Drona approached Yudhishthira because he had full trust in Yudhishthira. When Drona asked for the truth, Yudhishthira responded with, "Ashwatthama is dead, not sure, if man or elephant”, adding the word elephant indistinctly so that Drona could not hear it. Then Drona descended from his chariot, laid down his arms and sat on the ground in meditation to find his son's soul. Dhrishtadyumna took this opportunity and beheaded him.[1] This story is a good reminder that we must not trust everyone and never trust a person blindly. If Drona had cross-checked instead of blindly believing Yudhisthir, he would have not only saved his life but also given victory to the Kauravas. Hence, trusting everyone is a huge weakness, and you better overcome this weakness and learn to trust only those who are trustworthy, and never trusting anyone blindly. Question: How do politicians become wealthy when they enter politics? Is it possible for them to serve public interests instead of self-interests?
Answer: The British politician and writer Lord Acton immortalised himself in one quote: “Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.” This power is often used to explain why even good people become corrupt when they achieve power. However, I disagree with Lord Acton and must say that it is not the power that corrupts people but the nation's political environment. If power had been made the people corrupt, all the presidents, ministers and civil servants worldwide would have been corrupt. However, we know that the top politicians and civil servants of many countries like Singapore, Sweden, and Switzerland are known for their integrity despite enjoying the same powers as any other nation like India or Pakistan. The reality is that the country's political-administrative environment corrupts politicians and civil servants. Let me explain how the environment has a more powerful impact on corrupting a person than power. According to the Centre for Media Studies report, in the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, around Rs 55,000 crore, or $8 billion, was spent, and the Bharatiya Janata Party spent roughly half of that.[1] This is a staggering amount of money, around Rs 100 crores per Lok Sabha constituency. The legal limit for an election is only Rs 95 lakhs per candidate[2], and the total recorded money spent by all parties on elections is hardly 5% of this amount. It means that almost 95% of the money spent in elections is black money, which was collected and spent in cash. It is no wonder that before every election, hundreds of crores of money, a small portion of the total cash spent, are seized. For instance, recently, in Karnataka, a single seizure of ₹558 crore, the highest-ever pre-poll seizure, was made, in addition to the seizure of goods worth ₹348.71 crore by the Commercial Taxes Department. [3] This cash is surely given by the businessmen, who must have been given some favours by politicians and the top ministers in the government. According to the law, if any money is collected (for self or party) in lieu of any favour done to any person by a public servant (whether a politician or civil servant), it is covered under corruption. It is important to understand that it is immaterial whether or not the politician has personally benefited from this illegal transaction; he will suffer the same punishment as the politician who has taken part of the money for himself. Now, when you join politics and become a minister, one of your important tasks is to collect funds for the party from the businessmen. This illegal money will come only when you provide them with some illegal benefit, which may include protection from the investigation, award of tenders, etc. So, as a rational person, a politician would think that if I have to do this illegal act anyway and suffer jail, whether or not I take any money for myself, why not take at least a part of the money myself and protect my future, in case I lose power tomorrow. Most top politicians in India are known to be honest at a personal level. No one can accuse the prime ministers of India, such as Atal Bihari Vajpayee, Dr Manmohan Singh, or Mr Narendra Modi, of being corrupt at a personal level, as they never made any money for themselves. However, they all compromised to collect funds for the party. Similarly, there is no allegation or proof that top AAP leaders like Arvind Kejriwal or Manish Sisodia made any money for themselves. However, these AAP leaders may have to go to jail and face up to 7 years of imprisonment by the courts under the Prevention of Corruption Act because they misused their powers to collect funds for their party. It is, therefore, not surprising that most Indian politicians tend to make illegal money for themselves and their families due to the corrupt political-administrative environment of India, which has become so bad that you can’t win any election without the use of illegal money. If we want honest people to come to Indian politics, we have to clean up the country's political environment by enacting political reforms, like providing state funding for elections and curbing the misuse of illegal money in elections. However, I am not optimistic that such reforms will ever come to India because this corruption benefits the ruling party most, and they are the only political party that can bring such reforms.
