Question: Can wealth be considered an illusion of freedom and happiness?
Answer: If you go to an Indian market, it is common to see many old people selling vegetables and misc. items in cold winters, hot sun and rainy weather. While people usually retire at the age of 60 years, these poor people have no retirement life, and they have to work almost till the end of their lives. They have to open their shops almost every day and work from morning to evening, and they never experience rest and leisure in their life. On the other side, you find many people who work for a few years and then enjoy themselves for rest of their lives. What differentiates these two types of people is wealth. I have worked in the government service for 25 years and took voluntary retirement in 2016, while I still had 11 years of service left. Since, then I have been living a life of freedom and happiness, and doing only what I love to do, thanks to my savings and decent pension. During the post-retirement period, I have authored seven books, taught online, set up my own online teaching platform and written more than 4000 answers on Quora. A few months back, I spent two and half months in Europe visiting my daughter who is in Munich, Germany. I walk every day, read and write books, post answers on Quora, watch my favourite programmes on television without any time restrictions, take siesta every afternoon, go to the Gym in the evening, and practice piano daily for a couple of hours. Do you think, I could have done all that without wealth? We all have only one life. We all wish to enjoy happiness in our lives and achieve freedom to do what we love to do. Unfortunately, most people spend almost all their lives only earning their living doing jobs they hate to do. They spend almost all their income enjoying luxuries like big cars and expensive phones, eating food in expensive locations, drinking expensive wine, buying expensive branded clothes and going on foreign vacations. And, to pay for these luxuries, they have to work even harder doing what they hate to do, leaving even less free time to do what they want to do and enjoy happiness in life. As a result, they lead miserable lives despite earning a very good income. Even people earning modest incomes often waste lots of their money on drinking, instead of saving for the future. They even take loans to pay for their luxuries, addiction and show-off activities, which have to pay with high interest later. And when they retire at the age of 60, their health is failing, their children are already gone, and they have lost the desire and ability to enjoy their freedom. Wealth is not an illusion, but the most reliable source for enjoying freedom and happiness. A pauper can neither enjoy freedom nor happiness ever in his or her life. So, learn to live a simple life and save enough wealth at an early age so that you can quit the job you hate, and live a good life doing what you love to do for the rest of your life. Question: Why can’t the world be educated into not pressuring people into their own beliefs and not shaming them because they have a different opinion?
Answer: Belief is defined the feeling of being certain that something exists or is true. Thus belief is based on feelings and emotions rather than facts substantiated by reason or evidence. Beliefs are therefore always subjective as they are based on emotions. Unfortunately, most people treats their beliefes as true or facts, while question and redicule other people's beliefs. No amount of logic, evidence or reason can make a believer change his beliefs. So , let us first investigate what is the difference between a belief and a fact. Facts are objective and they remain same for everybody. For example, for example, 2 + 2=4 is a fact. Similarly, ‘the capital of India is Delhi’ is also a fact. The scientific principles like Newton's law, Faraday's law etc. are also facts because they are same for everybody and anybody can verify them. On the contrary, beliefs are subjective and needs no proof, for instance, belief in God. Different beliefs leads to different practices. For example, There is no way, you can find a way that is acceptable to all religions. Hence, conflicts between believers are inevitable. At the most, they can tolerate each other, but they can never respect each other or follow a common practice. Such relationship is always fragile, which can flare up at the slightest provocation. The only way to avoid conflict is to get rid of beliefs formed without evidence by developing rational thinking and and focusing on facts, which are same for everybody. Once everybody learns to form beliefs based on facts and evidence, all beliefs will be aligned in the society and harmony shall prevail in the world.

Question: What is the future of secularism in India, given the current political and social climate?
Answer: Secularism is an ideology that emphasizes the separation of religion and the state and the neutrality of the government with respect to religious beliefs. It has broadly two meanings: The Indian constitution aims for a secular state where all religions are treated equally[1] The word ‘secular’ was not part of the original Constitution, but was inserted with the Forty-second Amendment of the Constitution of India enacted in 1976 in the Preamble. However, the Supreme Court of India in the 1994 case S. R. Bommai v. Union of India established the fact that India was secular since the formation of the republic. The judgement established that there is separation of state and religion. It stated "In matters of State, religion has no place. Any State government which pursues nonsecular on policies or nonsecular course of action acts contrary to the constitutional mandate and renders itself amenable to action under Article 356".[2] Secular means not having any connection with religion. However, most Indians believe in God and say religion is very important in their lives. Nearly all Indians say they believe in God (97%), and roughly 80% of people in most religious groups say they are absolutely certain that God exists. [3] Can you have secularism in a country where 97% of people believe in God? It is a wonder that for more than half a century post-independence, Indian leaders broadly practised secularism by treating all religions equally and also maintaining equal distance from all religions in the matter of governance. They participated in Ram Lila but also participated in Iftar parties, Christmas and Guru Purnima. However, at present, most of the Governments in India, particularly the BJP governments at the Centre and states are openly siding with the majority religion Hinduism, which constitutes 80% of the population. In fact, the Pran Patishtha ceremony of the Ayodhya Ram Mandir inauguration on 22nd January 2024 was performed by PM Modi, UP CM Yogi, RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat and Anandiben Paten (Governor of UP).[4] The popularity of the BJP has skyrocketed after the inauguration of the Ram Temple, and they are almost sure to win the 2024 elections with a thumping majority. It is said that democracy is the dictatorship of the majority. When 97% of Indians are religious and 80% of Indians are devout Hindus, secularism hardly has any future in India. A democratic nation can’t be secular unless the majority of citizens are secular. Indians can become secular only when they develop rational thinking and scientific temper, which is incompatible with religious faith. Hence, secularism is practically dead in India, and now only formalities are required to remove the word “secular” from the Indian constitution and make it officially a religious state.

Question: What are some good things that I can learn from you?
Answer: A decade ago, I was posted as Commissioner of the Large Taxpayer Unit (LTU) in Chennai. One day an officer asked me if I wanted to visit Tirupati Balaji Temple. I told him that I had visited the temple in 1992 when I was a probationer. It took almost 6 hours to get Darshan, despite paying a special darshan fee. For the people seeking free darshan, it used to take 24 hours or even more. He said that I didn’t have to worry about the queue as he would arrange the VIP pass for our family. I discussed the proposed visit with my family, and they all happily agreed to visit Tirupati. Thereafter, the VIP pass was arranged and we visited the temple on the next week. We had a great experience visiting the temple. There was hardly any queue, and we could enter in the Sanctum Santorum within minutes. There was no pushing of the devotee. The priest asked us our name and Gotra and got the puja done on our behalf. We were feeling at the top of the world by getting the privilege. There are several types of Darshan in Tirupati Balaji Temple.[1] The main types are as follows. Even VIP Break Darshan had three categories Now, there is a Srivani Trust VIP Break Darshan, where a pilgrim who donates an amount of Rs. 10,000 will be provided a VIP darshan the next day with Rs. 500 for the VIP Darshan ticket.[3] We got special treatment in Tirupati Balaji Temple because we got L1 passes. If you are an ordinary person who can’t afford the darshan fee of Rs 300 or Rs 10,000, you might feel bad when compared to the people standing in the special darshan queue, who will be feeling jealous of the devotees having VIP Darshan. Even within the VIP category, the L3 will feel inferior compared to L2, who would feel inferior to L1 VVIP. Thus unless you are a VVIP, you will be likely to feel angry at the privilege given to the VVIPs in India, who have to barely stand for an hour to get the darshan and pray to the Lord according to the rituals. Most people are unhappy when they find people with more privileges and then they work hard to acquire these privileges for themselves and their family. When they fail to get these privileges, they feel angry, unhappy and frustrated. They often curse the world for being unfair and unjust. Can we have an alternative approach to life to get rid of this anger and frustration, and live a happy and peaceful life? Now, if you are an atheist, a Non-Hindu or a Hindu who does not believe in Idol worship or believe that God is everywhere and not only in a specific temple, you would never visit the temple, even if you get a VVIP pass, or even paid for your visit because even a VVIP has to spend lots of money and time to visit Tirupati and get Darshan. The visit can give you satisfaction and joy, only when you are highly religious and have a deep desire to visit the temple. If you have no desire to visit a temple and have darshan, all these privileges have no attraction for you, and billions of people around the world have no desire to visit the Tirupati Balaji Temple or any other religious places. It is important to realise that all human desires like the desire to have darshan in the temple, wealth, power, honour, fame etc. are self-created imaginary desires and not natural like the desire for food, water, clothing and shelter. If you seek the fulfilment of all your self-created desires, you can never be happy, because no person can ever fulfil all his desires. However, if you understand that all these desires are artificial and imaginary creations of your own mind, and you choose to give up the desires, you achieve happiness and satisfaction immediately. The worst thing is these imaginary desires keep on increasing as you fulfil them, and become greed which can never be satisfied. The German-American social philosopher Erich Fromm wisely said, “Greed is a bottomless pit which exhausts the person in an endless effort to satisfy the need without ever reaching satisfaction”. Hence, we must, instead of striving to fulfil our desires, strive to reduce our desire to live a happy and fulfilled life.

Question: Which is better: an arranged marriage or a love marriage?
Answer: The concept of arranged marriages has evolved so much in the last couple of decades in India that now there is hardly any difference between the two. My parents had arranged marriage in 1963. In those days the boy and the girl had no role in marriage. My father was studying in class XI while my mother after passing her class V, was trained to be a housewife by her mother. The grandfather of my mother met the grandfather of my father through some intermediary, and they settled the marriage. My father opposed the marriage, but he had to follow the commitment of his grandfather and get married. They have been happily married for 60 years. I had no girlfriend as in those days the interaction between boys and girls was almost non-existent, particularly for engineering students. There were only around half a dozen girls in our entire batch of 300+ in IIT-BHU (1983), and none in Mechanical Engineering. So, my marriage was to be arranged only. However, I was already selected in civil services then and had financial independence. So, I insisted on seeing the girl before giving my consent. My father hated the idea but had to give in. I already got lots of proposals, so I met a couple of girls in their home with my family and then finally selected my wife. During the entire process, it was the family members who connected with the boy and girl, and the boy and the girl hardly got an opportunity to talk to each other in private. Our first meeting was like in the following picture. Thus, I had to make the most important decision of my life based on a few minutes of interaction with the prospective wife and their family. My wife did not have even the privilege to consent and she had to get married to the first boy who was chosen by her father and accepted the proposal. Later, we had an arranged marriage in 1992, and now we have been happily married for 32 years. Question: Is too much discipline harmful?
Answer: A few months ago, I visited Munich (Germany) to stay with my children and visited many places in Germany and other countries of Europe. Germany is a beautiful and developed country, where everything seems to be perfect for an Indian like me. (Picture above: Neuschwanstein Castle in Germany) Everyone in Germany appears to be so disciplined, civilised and well-mannered that you can’t help admiring the people and the nation. However, just a couple of days later, we saw the other side of discipline when we visited a place named Dachau, near Munich, which has one of the first concentration camps built by Nazi Germany and the longest-running one.[1] The prisoners here lived in constant fear of brutal treatment and terror detention including standing cells, floggings, the so-called tree or pole hanging, and standing at attention for extremely long periods. There were 32,000 documented deaths at the camp and thousands that are undocumented. Approximately 10,000 of the 30,000 prisoners were sick at the time of liberation.[2] It reminded me of how Hitler was able to organise millions of disciplined Germans to start World War II, the largest and most violent military conflict in human history, which led to the death of 55 million people, including the deaths of 6 million Jews in the Holocaust. [3] Discipline is a twin-edged sword. Too much discipline can thus cause huge destruction of human values because with excessive discipline, humans can become machines and they can kill anyone without any guilt at the order of the authority. Germany and Japan are among the most disciplined countries in the world, but they caused huge destruction in the world in the last century as their disciplined people had never learned to question the orders of their masters. Discipline may be necessary, as without discipline, there can be no order in society and no social progress would be possible. However, too much discipline tends to reduce human rationality and kills creativity, innovation, humanity, love and compassion. The best course is, therefore, to educate and develop rational thinking in the people to cultivate self-discipline so that they are driven to do the right things due to their inner conviction rather than due to the fear of authority. Edit Post World War, Germany and Japan became liberal democracies while remaining disciplined, which lead to a balance of discipline and liberty, and made them developed countries within a few decades. Today, their citizens are self-disciplined which makes their development and prosperity sustainable. On the other hand, Russia (erstwhile USSR) maintained hard discipline post World War, which led to their rapid development, and its rise as Superpower. However, they could not sustain the momentum which lead to their disintegration and decline. China enforced strict discipline after the Tiananmen Square protest/massacre (1989), which lead to its rapid development and its emergence as the second largest economy in the world and one of the most powerful countries in the world. However, if some amount of liberty is not infused, too much discipline can lead to the decline of China in future. Source of picture: Google Images

Question: How do you feel when someone says “Two wrongs don’t make a right”?
Answer: The saying “two wrongs don’t make a right” means that it is not acceptable to do something bad to someone just because they did something bad to you first. The saying implies that we should be good to everyone, including those who have been bad to us. The logic behind this saying is that if we do bad even to pay back a bad person in the same coin, we become bad ourselves. For example, if someone kills your family member and you in return him or his family member, you too become a murderer just like him, and thus a bad person. Then what is the difference between that person and you? THIS SAYING THUS TELLS US WHAT IS NOT TO BE DONE WITHOUT TELLING US WHAT SHOULD WE DO WHEN SOMEONE DOES BAD TO US. IT THUS REPRESENTS ONLY HALF-TRUTH. Justice demands that we should appropriately treat people. The Old Testament, capture this natural human emotion as it asks us to pay back the evil person in the same coin i.e. "a life for a life— eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound,” ( Exodus 21: 24–25). However, if people pay evil with evil, the evil will spread and the world will be filled with more evil. Mahatma Gandhi therefore warned, “An eye for an eye will leave everyone blind.” So, what should we do, when someone does wrong to us? Jesus Christ, suggested the opposite, “You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye, and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you, do not resist an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to them the other cheek also. And if anyone wants to sue you and take your shirt, hand over your coat as well. (Matthew 5:38-40) Hence, we are confused when dealing with people who do wrong to us. This issue has been debated for thousands of years, and we have yet to come to any conclusion. Let us examine which of the theory is practical when tested in a real-world situation. Hitler started the Second World War which led to the death of almost 65 million people worldwide and the destruction of most of Europe. However, Gandhi, a believer in nonviolence and the ‘two-wrongs-do-not-make-it-right, suggested that British people should not use violence against Nazis. Accordingly, he wrote an open letter to the British people dated 2.7.1940, ”I want you to fight Nazism without arms, or, if I am to retain the military terminology, with non-violent arms. I would like you to lay down the arms you have as being useless for saving you or humanity. You will invite Herr Hitler and Signor Mussolini to take what they want of the countries you call your possessions. Let them take possession of your beautiful island, with your many beautiful buildings. You will give all these but neither your souls, nor your minds. If these gentlemen choose to occupy your homes, you will vacate them. If they do not give you free passage out, you will allow yourself man, woman and child, to be slaughtered, but you will refuse to owe allegiance to them.”[1] Imagine the consequence of following Gandhi’s advice! It is good that the British and the Allied forces did not follow Gandhi’s advice, or else the world would have been ruled by Nazis today. An evil man like Hitler would only listen to the eye-for-eye policy, and ultimately, he could be defeated by paying him the same coin. Hence, in this case, two wrongs made the right, and violence has eliminated violence in Europe, which has had unparalleled peace for more than 70 years since the World War. When someone says “Two wrongs don’t make a right”, I feel that the person is a coward, or an idealist who has little experience of the real world. While we must try to avoid doing wrong deeds every time we are wronged, and try to persuade, convince and reform the wrongdoer to making him understand his mistake and mend his ways usingpeaceful means, we must also be ready to pay the wrongdoer in the same coin, if the need arises. Hence, it is evident that, In a civilised society, the retaliatory evil is committed by the State on behalf of the victim by lawfully awarding imprisonment, penalty or death. However, when the State fails to correct the wrong against its citizens, the victim is forced to take the law into their own hands and correct the wrong himself by committing a similar wrong to the perpetrator of evil. Hence, the philosophy of two wrongs do not make it right can be followed only in a society in which the rule of law is followed and the state takes the responsibility or corrects the wrong by punishing the wrongdoer. Question: What are some interesting & amazing facts that most people don't know?
Answer: Let me share with you something amazing that I learned recently. Please answer the following question. Approximately 1% of women aged 40-50 have breast cancer. A woman with breast cancer has a 90% chance of a positive test from a mammogram, while a woman without has a 10% chance of a false positive result. What is the probability a woman has breast cancer given that she just had a positive test? When I was asked this question, I thought this to be a simple problem. I did my mental calculation and my estimate was around 70–80%. Perhaps, your estimate is also something close. Even experts also gave similar estimates. When ninety-five physicians were asked this question their average answer was 75%. [1] However, we are not only wrong in our estimation of the probability but so grossly wrong that it may surprise us. The correct answer is that the woman has just a 8% chance of having breast cancer. So, what is happening? How come even the experts are so wrong about the calculation of the real chances of getting breast cancer? The misjudgement happens because of our tendency to ignore relevant statistical information in favour of case-specific information. Instead of taking into account the base rate or prior probability of an event, we are often distracted by less relevant information. Our inability to consider the prior probability or the base is also called the base rate fallacy. In statistics, base rate refers to the percentage of a population that has a specific characteristic. If we take a random individual and there’s no additional information, the base rate tells us the likelihood of them demonstrating that characteristic. In this case, we have not taken into account the fact that only 1% of women have breast cancer. Let me explain how to understand and solve this problem. Suppose that the sample size is 1000. Since only 1% of the women have breast cancer, hence, there would be 10 women with breast cancer and 990 women without breast cancer. When these 990 women were tested, 99 got positive cancer reports without any cancer, while 9 women who actually got cancer reported correctly. Hence, while only 10 women have cancer, the total number of detection would be 99+9=108. Hence, the probability of those who have been tested positive and have breast is just 9/108 which is around 8%. I found this piece of knowledge truly amazing. The correct calculation of the probability is done by Bayesian inference in which Bayes' theorem is used to update the probability for a hypothesis as more evidence or information becomes available. Bayesian inference uses prior knowledge, in the form of a prior distribution in order to estimate posterior probabilities. You can solve this problem directly by using Bayes’ formula. The knowledge of the base rate fallacy is essential for correctly estimating the possibility and avoiding wrong decisions in life. For example, one lesson is that you must not undertake routine tests for a disease like breast cancer which is quite less prevalent, unless you have symptoms. Moreover, if you test positive in such cases, better to get tested again to avoid a false positive. Some examples of operating base rate fallacy are as follows. I hope you have found this information interesting and useful, and you can use this to find answers to many problems in your life and take the correct decisions.

Question: Is it possible a good human may do bad things or an ex criminal may do good things later in their lives?
Answer: It is not only possible but most probable. As a matter of fact, in statistics, there is a well-laid-down principle called “regression toward the mean” (also called reversion to the mean, and reversion to mediocrity). According to this principle, the phenomenon where if one sample of a random variable is extreme, the next sampling of the same random variable is likely to be closer to its mean.[1] Hence, a good human being is more likely to commit bad things in future and a bad person is more likely to commit good things in future. Let us look at the spring in the picture, pressed by both hands You have reduced the length of the spring by applying external force. How long can you press this spring? As soon as you release the pressure, the spring will go to the other extreme, and then gradually come back to its natural state, and surely have a longer length (original) as compressed to its length in the pressed state. Similarly, if you elongate the spring with external force, again it will return to its natural state, as soon as it is released and become shorter. Human nature is composed of both good and evil. What we call evil is actually the original nature of the person (basic instinct), while what we call good is cultivated in human beings through education and training (learned instinct). Throughout our lives, we have to balance our good and evil nature to lead a natural life. When you suppress the original nature of the person by force, it is like pressing the spring, which always tries to come back to the original self as soon as the opportunity arises. Similarly, if you have been doing bad things in life, like engaging in crime or corruption, you feel very uncomfortable in your subconscious mind due to the guilt and you try to do something good to overcome your guilt and acquire your original conscience (also called prayaschit in Sanskrit meaning getting back to prior/original conscience). It has been my experience that in the real world, honest people are more inclined to become corrupt because they see them enjoying their lives with huge ill-gotten wealth (which they always lack). On the other side, the corrupt and wealthy people envy the honest people who are trusted, admired and loved by others and sleep well due to their clear conscience and honest living. Unfortunately, crime and corruption are a one-way path. An honest person can become corrupt or criminal by a single action, but a criminal and corrupt person can never become a good person even if does numerous good deeds. It is always easy to fall, but difficult to rise. Hence, if you have been a good person, don’t allow the temptation and lust to commit evil acts. And if you have done bad things in life, it is never too late to become a good person. Saint Augustine said so wisely, “Every saint has a past and every sinner has a future.” Source of picture: Google Images

Question: If money brings happiness then why the richest persons are still not happy?
Answer: In order to understand why money can’t buy happiness, we have to understand happiness itself. Happiness is often defined as a positive emotional state characterized by feelings such as contentment, joy, and life satisfaction. Human desires are at the root of happiness as well as suffering. For instance, hunger is the source of pain, which millions of poor people around the world feel every day. If you don’t get food when you are hungry, your pain of hunger continues to increase, and it may become unbearable if you don’t get food even for a day. However, the same hunger becomes the source of your joy, when your hunger is satisfied as you eat the food of your choice. Imagine that by some boon, you get rid of hunger. Now, you will never feel the pain of hunger, but you will also not find any joy in eating to satisfy your hunger. Hence, our hunger, or the need is the source of our pain (unsatisfied needs) as well as happiness (satisfied needs). Maslow provided a hierarchy of needs comprising a five-tier model of human needs, often depicted as hierarchical levels within a pyramid. The five levels of the hierarchy are physiological, safety, love/belonging, esteem, and self-actualization, as shown in the figure below. According to this theory, the lower-level basic needs like food, water, and safety must be met first before higher needs can be fulfilled.[1] If we look at the bottom of the pyramid, we find physiological & safety and security needs, which are physical/material, and thus can be easily satisfied with money. Most people in the world don’t have enough money to satisfy these basic needs itself, because they don’t have enough money to have good food, clothing, house, jobs, security etc. Hence, for most of the people, money indeed brings happiness. However, once you have enough wealth to satisfy your physical and safety needs, your higher-level needs (love and belonging, self-esteem and self-actualisation) come into existence. Unfortunately, the higher level needs are not material in nature, and thus can’t be purchased with any amount of money. Pat Williams wisely writes in “What Are You Living For?: Investing Your Life in What Matters Most” “Money can buy a house, but not a home; a bed, but not rest; food, but not an appetite; medicine, but not health; information, but not wisdom; thrills, but not joy; associates, but not friends; servants, but not loyalty; flattery, but not respect.” As a result, most wealthy people feel frustrated, when they can’t fulfil their higher-level needs of love, self-esteem and self-actualisation with all their money. Often, in their quest to make more and more wealth, they have permanently lost the possibility of the fulfilment of higher-level needs. Hence, the wealth that the rich people thought would make them happy, actually becomes the source of their misery, if acquired through the wrong means or by sacrificing their responsibilities towards their loved ones. These rich people then live the rest of their lives with the realisation that money can’t bring happiness, and they even blame money for their pain and suffering. Jesus Christ warned people about this fetal error, “What good will it be for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul? Or what can anyone give in exchange for their soul?” (Matthew 16:26) It is wise to remember that money is necessary for happiness as without money you can’t satisfy your physical and security needs. However, if you acquire money through the wrong means, or by sacrificing your personal life, all the wealth of the world can’t give you lasting happiness as higher-level needs can’t be purchased with any amount of wealth.

Question: What is love?
Answer: Love is the most used (and misused) word in the world. People use the word ‘love’ to refer to anything that creates positive feelings in them. For example, Love can be even used for most animalistic feeling like having sex (We make love), and also with the most exalted feeling (Love is God) Love has become the most common word to express all types of ‘feel good’ emotions, which happens when your desires are satisfied. When love is based on desires, it is temporary, because as soon as the desire is satisfied, the feelings evaporate, just like you don’t feel hungry once you have eaten the food. Hence, people fall out of love soon, because their loved one is unable to fulfil his or her desire. Ambrose Bierce even defined love as 'A temporary insanity curable by marriage.' However, wise people have warned that ‘love’ is not easy, but actually the most difficult emotions. The Indian poet Mirza Ghalib wrote, Ye ishq nahīñ āsāñ itnā hī samajh liije ik aag kā dariyā hai aur Duub ke jaanā hai English Translation ‘Love is not easy. Understand it like this. It is a river of fire, and you have to cross it from within ’ So, what is love? Clearly, every positive feeling is not love. I am no ‘love guru’, but let me share my opinion about love. Love in my opinion is ‘mutual possessiveness’, or ‘mutual ownership’. It means that when you love someone, you allow your loved one to possess you or own you. There is no love without the feeling of possession or ownership. You can love only what is yours. Imagine, you visit a car showroom and see many beautiful cars there.[1] You may like all the beautiful cars, but you don’t love them unless you own them. Only when you buy a car, or in some other way own it, you can love your car, even if it is small, or old. Same way, you can only love your house, your clothes, and your country, because you feel that you own them and being the owner, you have the power to claim the thing to be your own, and you are also responsible for its well-being. Let us now discuss our love for people. When you say that you love a person (parent, children, spouse, beloved, friend) you must have a feeling of ownership or right over that person, and at the same time, you allow the person to have the right over you. For example, if you love your mother, and you say to your mother: “Mom, I want to eat such and such food’, you know that your mother will cook the food you love and treat your will as a command, despite being your mother, and her power to say no. In the same way, if your mother says, ‘Can you take me to the market’, she knows that she has a right over you, and you will not refuse her unless of course there are some genuine reasons for saying no, which must be convincing to her. Hence, if you love someone, you surrender your independence to her will, and obey her will like a command coming from the most powerful person, like your boss. Similarly, to every person whom you love, you allow himself or herself to be your master. So, according to the mutual possessiveness principle of love It is for this reason, love is very difficult, because ‘independence’ is the most important ingredient for happiness, and you have to surrender your liberty to every person you love. In other words, you make yourself obliged to serve every person you love. The more people you love, the less freedom you have to live your life in your own way. So, if your little daughter says that she wants an ice cream, or wants to go out in your car, you will follow her orders, and do exactly what she wants, unless of course the demand is bad for her, or you have something very important thing to do. Sufferings due to Love Love can thus become a great suffering sometimes, because by loving a person you make your loved one your master and become a servant, but that does not necessarily mean that your beloved would love you back and consider your will as her command. Aristotle beautifully said, "Love is composed of a single soul inhabiting two bodies." Hence, when you love someone, you unilaterally allow that person to control your soul, feelings and emotions and thus give her the power to hurt you, either by hurting you directly or even by hurting herself in any way. Hence, love is not only a source of happiness but also a great source of suffering. Love not only gives you the power to control other people but also makes you forgo your liberty and be controlled by your loved one. Be aware that love is a great responsibility, and one must be very careful to love someone or seek someone’ love. If you love the right person, your life is heaven, and if you love the wrong person, your life can become hell.

Question: If honesty is the best policy, why do honest people suffer more?
Answer: There is a famous idiom related to journalism, "When a dog bites a man, that is not news, because it happens so often. But if a man bites a dog, that is news." The idiom describes how an unusual, infrequent event (such as a man biting a dog) is more likely to be reported as news than an ordinary, everyday occurrence such as a dog biting a man. The narrative that honest people suffer more than the dishonest people is because the facts that we know through the popular media is not the reality, but an exception. For example, when people like Mahatma Gandhi becomes the greatest leader of the world of 20th century, or Dr Lal Bahadur Shastri becomes the Prime Minister of India or Dr Kalam becomes the President of India, it is never a news because people believe that they all deserve the position and honour. Similarly, every year thousands of honest students get selected into the civil services at various level purely due to their hard work and honesty, it never makes a news, as it is normal. However, when one honest IAS officer like Ashok Khemka is frequently transferred, or one Satyndra Dubey is killed for doing is work honestly, or some students get selected based on leaked paper or cheating, it becomes a news because honest people suffering is an exception. Similarly, when dishonest people suffer in life, it hardly makes a news, because that is what is normal. There are millions of people around the world inside the jail because they committed crimes, corruption or fraud, and many of them would even die within the jail. Most of them are even discarded by their family and friends. However, their suffering does not make a news, as bad people suffering is normal in the world. However, when good people like Mahatma Gandhi, Nelson Mandela are imprisoned, it becomes a news and widely reported in the press and media. Due to the cognitive bias called availability bias (or availability heuristic), humans have the tendency to rely on information that is easier to recall when faced with a decision, rather than getting the full facts of the case by collecting complete information about the reality. Hence, most people give disproportionate importance to the exceptions (which rarely happens) than then normal (which happens all the time). The phenomenon is also described in the journalistic saying, "You never read about a plane that did not crash." However, it does not mean that plane crash is more common that planes that land safely to the destination. Hence, the saying that honesty is the best policy holds good today as much as it was valid in the past, and it shall remain valid in future as well. However, it is foolish to expect that just because you are honest, you will not suffer pain and failure in life and always enjoy success and happiness. Just like you can’t achieve success in any examination just because you are honest (you don’t cheat), unless you also know the subject well better than others, you also can’t achieve success in life unless you work hard to acquire the knowledge and skill to outperform others. Honest people often suffer because they are so much infatuated by their honesty that they don’t give enough attention for improving their skills and deliver better results in their profession. However, when they fail, instead of blaming their incompetency, prefer to play victim and ascribe their honesty for their failure. Honesty is thus a necessary, but not a sufficient condition for happiness and success. To lead a good life, you must not only be honest, but also hardworking, able and competent to produce results and deliver excellence. Question: Why is it often said that we learn from our mistakes? Can we learn from others' experiences instead of making our own mistakes?
Answer: Let me tell you “The secrets of success” before answering the question. “Sir, what is the secret of your success?” a reporter asked a bank president. “Two words.” “And, Sir, what are they?” asked the reporter. “Right decisions.” “And how do you make right decisions?” “One word.” “What is that, Sir?” “Experience.” “And how do you get Experience?” the reporter asked. “Two words.” “And, Sir, what are they?” “Wrong decisions.”[1] Learning from other’s experiences without making mistakes is like hoping to get cured of your illness and become healthy by administering medicine to a healthy person. You can acquire valuable lessons in life only by experience. And you can gain experience only through the extensive practice of the knowledge acquired by you. You are sure to commit mistakes in the process of learning, and if you keep learning from your mistakes, you will gradually master the craft and develop the skill of doing things in the right way. Let me explain this with the help of a practical and personal example. I have been learning piano online for the last six months from an online course from a young professional pianist and coach “Jash Gotawala”, the founder of the ed-tech platform Pix series. I first tried to hire a tutor to teach me piano, but could not get a good one in Lucknow. Then I came to know about Jash Gotawala and his YouTube Channel, where he has posted hundreds of videos for learning piano. For example, in the following video, he teaches the complete piano course in just 3 hours. Now, when you see him playing the piano, it seems like a play, as he effortlessly plays even complex songs with chords and Arpeggio. However, when you actually try to play the song yourself, you understand the difficulty. First of all, you can’t pick up the right notes for songs. If you memorise these notes and try to play, your figures of right hands don’t move swiftly according to the rhythm of the song. And how many notes, you can memorise? When you try to use the left-hand fingers to play the chord or Arpeggio, your right-hand stops playing the correct notes, and when you focus on the right hand, the left hand loses its rhythm. If you have ever tried to play the piano, or for that matter any musical instrument, you know how difficult it is to learn to play even the simplest instrument. Initially, you commit so many mistakes while attempting to play the instrument that you even lose hope that you will ever be able to play the instrument. However, if you don’t lose hope, and keep playing, your mistakes will reduce over time and then one day you will be able to play the instrument as effortlessly as a professional. Can you learn the piano simply by watching the video and learning from the experience of the master? In my opinion, if you watch all the videos a million times, you will still not be able to learn the basics of piano. You have to actually play the piano and commit thousands of mistakes in the process and correct those mistakes to learn the piano. Just like you can’t learn swimming by watching professionals swim or driving by observing a professional driver driving the car, you can’t learn the lessons of life without doing the task yourself and committing mistakes. The experiences of others are valuable because they can expedite the process of learning, but ultimately you have to suffer the pain of failure yourself to learn any valuable lessons of life. So, instead of expecting to learn the piano by watching videos, I joined the online course on Pix Series and I am practising a couple of hours every day to learn the piano. I am well aware that it is going to take several months and even years to actually play the piano flawlessly like a professional. Unfortunately, there is no shortcut to success and skill development, except by committing mistakes, suffering failures and learning from each mistake. So, be ready to commit mistakes and suffer the pain of failure before you can enjoy the fruits of your labour and rewards of achievement.

Question: What is the biggest lesson you learned that no one teaches?
Answer: I used to teach essay writing for UPSC sometime back. One of the most important lessons that I used to give to my students is called the Peak-End Rule. When you write a long essay (1000–1200 words), you must keep the peak-end rule in mind because when an examiner finishes reading your essay and is about to award you the marks, he will not remember everything that you have written in your essay, but the peaks and the end. Accordingly, The same peak-end rule is applicable to our lives as well. Let us elaborate them now. 1: Peak rule We know that Mahatma Gandhi was one of the greatest world leaders of the 20th Century. When Time Magazine chose the top 100 persons of the 20th century, Mahatma Gandhi was only next to Albert Einstein, who was chosen as the Person of the Century.[1] Yet, if you study the life of Mahatma Gandhi, he is remembered today for at the most a dozen bold decisions in his public life of more than half a century, which translates to one memorable act per five years. Most people become immortal by their single act of greatness. For example, the American author Dale Carnegie has written almost a dozen books in his career between 1915 to 1962, but he is remembered today for just one book How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936). Einstein had written dozens of papers, but what made him world-famous was his theory of relativity. Hence, the first lesson is that instead of trying to do numerous ordinary things in life, try to do a few great things in life, and go deeper into it by spending considerable time to hone up your skill to develop excellence, which will give you lifelong satisfaction. 2: End-Rule We know the famous saying: “All is well that ends well.” Your lifetime of achievement means nothing if the end is bad, because people would not remember you for whatever great things you did in your life, but what had been your final achievement? You perhaps know this man. His name is Naresh Goyal, the founder of Jet Airways, which was one of the largest and best airlines in India just a decade ago. He started operating Jet Airways in 1993, and in 2005, Forbes magazine declared him the 16th richest person in India, with a net worth of US$1.9 billion. The following is the list of awards he received in his lifetime.[2] However, he was arrested by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) last year for an alleged fraud of ₹538 crore at the Canara Bank. A few days back, he was in the news because he broke down in court, saying he had ‘lost every hope of life’ and would be better if he died in jail than live in the present situation. He submitted to the court that he misses his wife Anita, who is in the advanced stage of cancer,.. his wife is bedridden and their only daughter is unwell.[3] Yesterday, the Mumbai court had allowed Naresh Goyal to attend his private doctors for diagnosis and to meet his bedridden wife.[4] No. Everyone will only remember his end, which was painful and ignominious. If Mr Goyal is given a second chance, he would prefer to live a simple life and die like an ordinary man rather than end his life with so much pain and infamy. There are numerous examples like Naresh Goyal, who achieved great success in life, but whose ending was very bad. Most people, however, don’t care about their future and indulge in fraud, adultery, corruption, and crimes, to achieve wealth, power and immoral pleasure. However, when they are caught, they have to pay a huge price for their misadventure and then all their repentance and guilt can never give them even an ordinary pleasure available to every ordinary person in the world, like freedom, time to spend with family and live peacefully. So, don’t follow the rat race and don’t commit acts, which if exposed would ruin all your happiness, freedom and honour. You must ensure that whatever you start, you also end well since you will not be judged based on the sum total of your achievements, but only on your end. No one teaches you this peak-end rule of life, but if you remember, this can be one of the most valuable life lessons of your life.

So I did not take back the resignation, and finally, I was relieved of my job on 31st October, 2016. An American author Phil McGraw said, “Sometimes you make the right decision, sometimes you make the decision right.” In fact, there are no inherently right decisions till you make them right with your hard work and perseverance. So, if you wish to ignore public opinion and charter your own path, you have to develop tremendous confidence in yourself and your ability to work hard to fulfil the promises made to you. You have to start with simple decisions and make them right, and then gradually your confidence can grow to a level when you can develop a ‘don’t-give-damn’ attitude to the public opinion.

Question: What is your review of 12th Fail movie and the hype around it?
Answer: I watched the Hindi movie 12th Fail a few days ago on the OTT platform. I liked the movie but not the message that the movie tries to convey. Let me now explain why I disagree with the message. The Civil Services Examination is certainly one of the toughest examinations in the world with a rejection rate of over 99.9% (less than 1000 people get selected among one million applicants). It is perhaps the only examination in the world that can transform your life forever, and ensure you high status and lifetime job security. However, it is also a fact that you must be really a brilliant student to succeed in the examination. In this movie, a 12th failed student Manoj Kumar Sharma, who came from a very poor family background get selected into the Indian Police Service (IPS), in his last attempt, presumably at the age of 33 years since the maximum age for the general category candidate is 32 years. Here is the picture of real and reel life Manoj Sharma.[1] Imagine, if he was not selected for the civil services examination in the last attempt. What type of job he would have got, or career choices he would have? Should we encourage young people to spend a decade of their life to realise their dream of becoming a top civil servant? Does IAS/IPS/IFS/IRS are really worth the hype created in the movie? Unfortunately, every year, lakhs of students fail to make it to the civil services examination after almost a decade of effort motivated by such stories of exceptional success and ruin of their youth and life. The key message of the movie is that if a 12th fail can get selected into civil services, anyone can get selected. This message is wrong because your academic track record plays a very important role in your success in all competitive examinations, including CSE. I, for example, was selected for the civil services examination (IRS) in the first attempt itself in 1990, while doing my M-Tech at IIT Delhi. And I was not an exception. In those days more than 100 students (among 700 odd selections) were selected from IIT Delhi alone with hardly 400 students who appeared in the examination. If my memory serves me right, there were almost 15 ranks in the CSE from IIT in the top 20 in the year 1990 selection, most of them in their very first attempt. Thus the success percentage in IIT Delhi was more than 25% on those days, as against the overall success rate of less than 0.5%. Further, the maximum age for appearing in CSE in those days was only 26 years for the general category. Hence, the risk of taking civil services was minimal for IIT students as even those who failed to make it, could easily get jobs in academic or corporate. It is thus evident that academic brilliance plays a significant role in achieving success in CSE, and a brilliant student has at least 100 times more chance of selection than a 12th Fail sudent. Hence, if you have a poor track record in academics, you must understand that you are taking a huge risk by taking the civil services examination if you don’t have a backup option. If anyone collects the data of selection, I am sure it can be easily established that most people who get selected have consistently good academic records while most candidates with poor records may fail to even clear the Prelims in all their attempts. While the 12th Fail movie will motivate hundreds of thousands of young students to dedicate a decade of their lives to become a top civil servant, more than 99% per cent of them would repent their decision after a decade and ruin their lives. I am not discouraging the academically poor students from writing the CSE, but they must realistically evaluate their chances of success before attempting the examination. .

Question: Why do civil services posts have to follow the toughest examinations and politicians don't need any exams in order to be there?
Answer: The civil services examination indeed is one of the toughest examinations in the world. However, it is even more difficult to become a successful politician. The civil services examination has a well-defined syllabus and thousands of coaching institutes in the country that can help you score better marks in the competition and achieve success. Do you know any coaching institutes for training people to become great politicians? I am sure if any brilliant person can indeed set up such a coaching institute, it will be much more sought after than the coaching institute for civil servants. Why? Civil servants learn their lessons from books, but is easy, but politicians have to learn their lessons directly from the people, which is far more difficult. The power of civil servants for which millions try their luck is nothing compared to the power of the politicians. Most of you perhaps can identify this man. His name is Kishor Kanyal, the erstwhile District Collector of Sajapur district of MP, who was talking to the striking truckers on June 2, 2024. During the meeting, he lost his cool and shouted at a truck driver “Tumhari Aukat Kya Hai? (What is your status (before me)?)[1] However, once the video clip became viral, he was transferred from his post to the secretariate within 24 hours (and lost all his own aukat/status) by the Chief Minister of the State, the top politician of his state. This is the power of a politician. They can make the top civil servants totally powerless within no time. Imagine, how the Civil servants will behave with common people, if there are no politicians above them? The very purpose of democracy will be defeated. Hence, it is not a surprise that many top civil servants aspire to become politicians, once they realise their full power. However, they know that the competition for becoming a top politician is far more difficult than the competition they qualified for in their young days to become a civil servant. The civil servants have to take the examination only once in a lifetime and once they are selected, they can enjoy the pay perks and time-bound promotions throughout their lives. However, for politicians, the competition happens every five years, and they can become a zero, if they are defeated in the election if their party finds a better candidate for the job. There is no competition bigger than winning the hearts of the people because there are no syllabus, no books and no rules to win the hearts of the people. Have you ever found a written competition that is used to select the top actors, directors, leaders, entrepreneurs, writers, singers, or other artists? I know none. There can’t be a written competition to select the leaders, artists or entrepreneurs where you prepare the predefined syllabus and impress the examination to get the top job. A leader's job is to understand the needs of millions of people, connect with them emotionally and solve their problems. The competition politicians face is far tougher than the competition the civil servants face. There is a written competition for civil servants because they must be educated and intelligent enough to know the rules and laws of the country and help even an illiterate elected representative of the people to run the government in a democracy. However, the real responsibility to deliver the results lies on the politicians, who are elected in the toughest competition of the country called the election where millions of people assess them before casting their votes.

Question: Do we need knowledge or experience in order to have intellectual insights?
Answer: Neither knowledge nor experience can make you intellectual. However, in the real world, most intellectuals are young and from outside the academic world. It is so because intelligence is developed when we synthesise knowledge with experience. It means Mark Twain once explained the futility of experience unless we learn the right lessons: ‘We should be careful to get out of an experience only the wisdom that is in it – and stop there; lest we be like the cat that sits down on a hot stove lid. She will never sit down on a hot stove lid again – and that is well, but also she will never sit down on a cold one anymore.’ Hence, it is surprising that most people get senile with age, rather than becoming wise or intellectual, while a young person who learns the right lessons from each experience becomes wise at a young age. Similarly, the professors hardly know the secrets of life because they rarely put their knowledge into practice, and are thus equipped with only second-hand knowledge. The American aithor Neoplean Hill wisely said, “Knowledge is only potential power. It becomes power only when, and if, it is organized into definite plans of action, and directed to a definite end.” In simple words, knowledge is useless unless it is used to achieve a goal. We develop intellectual insights when we use our knowledge in action and then compare the outcome with the prediction, and fine tune what you know. Gradually, you will know whether or the acquired knowledge is true, discard the false knowledge, and develop the insight to use the knowledge in the right way.

Question: How do you explain karma? It doesn't make sense, but it is true.
Answer: Karma to me is the inevitability of the consequence of your action according to the laws of nature. If means you reap what you sow. Accordingly, I see the validity of the laws of karma almost every day, though it may take a long time, sometimes several years, for the seed of their actions to bear fruit. The people doing bad deeds are more likely to suffer bad consequences and those doing good deeds will enjoy their fruits of labour later. It is often argued that many bad people enjoy their life while many good people have to suffer in life, by giving selected anecdotal evidence of good people suffering and bad people living well. It is like arguing that many cigarette smokers don’t get cancer while many nonsmokers suffer from cancer. Such arguments are not correct because if you analyse large data, you will always find that the rate of cancer in smokers is almost 10 times more than the nonsmokers. Further, we often focus only on the negative deeds of a bad person who is living well, and the selected positive deeds of a good person who is suffering, without taking into consideration their holistic karma, which consists of good and bad. Hence, However, some people extend the theory of Karma to past lives and try to justify every unexplained thing to karma, instead of analysing the factors responsible for the event and the role of chance/probability, as I discussed in the case of smoking. I don’t believe in rebirth, the eternity of the soul and the concept of Sanchit Karma (the law of accumulated karma of the previous births), as they are a matter of faith, rather than based on any evidence or reason. For example, if an innocent girl is raped and murdered, or a person dies in a road accident, it is not due to her karma of the past life, but because of poor law and order, corruption in police and judiciary, not inculcating the right values in the men and the law of probability. Karma is thus a valid and good principle of nature that motivates people to be good, rather than convincing people that if they commit their evils smartly, they can avoid the consequences of their actions, and that good deeds are useless in this evil world. The laws of karma will surely catch you sooner or later, and you will reap the harvest of your good or evil karma. Question: What are some possible reasons why Indian political leaders are rarely punished for their corrupt practices?
Answer: Politicians are representatives of the people and the real rulers in a democracy. They make the law, head all the departments, and appoint the civil servants in the investigating agencies. No wonder, politicians hardly face punishment in India or anywhere in the world, for their crimes and corruption, unless they are targeted by rival politicians. Let us discuss the reasons why politicians are the most corrupt, but least punished community in the world. 1: Legal Loopholes Politicians make the laws through the legislature. All politicians need huge funds to fight elections and they are also obliged to return the favours to the corrupt businessmen and bureaucracies once they gain power. Hence, they make the laws which protect them. for example, in India, you need permission from the appointed authority (which is almost always politicians) to even start an investigation of a corruption case. After the investigation, again permission is needed to file a chargesheet. If they deny the permission, no investigation can even start against them or their favourite corrupt officers. 2: Control over Investigating Agencies All the investigating agencies empowered to investigate corruption cases are working under the politicians. Question: Why do people hate diversity equity and inclusion?
Answer: The terms diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) are often grouped together because they are interconnected and together they impact society in a big way. Let us understand the three terms and their use in the modern context.[1] 1: Diversity Diversity means that the workforce must be diverse, which means there should be diversity in terms of all genders (men, women, binary), age, ethnicity, physical ability and neurodiversity. 2: Equity Equity refers to a state that ensures equal opportunities for all. The concept recognises that privileges exist for some, and barriers exist for others. It integrates approaches to correct and equalise these inequalities (e.g., through quotas) or positive discrimination and prevent discrimination. Equity differs from equality. While equality assumes that all people should be treated the same, equity takes into consideration a person’s unique circumstances, adjusting treatment accordingly so that the end result is equal. 3: Inclusion Inclusion is about whether individuals feel included or excluded within a group. Even in a diverse environment, individuals can feel marginalised and excluded. Inclusion should, therefore, be promoted jointly with diversity.[2] While the intention of DEI appears to be Noble, in practice, it denies the people equality and justice in the name of equality and justice. When people are appointed on the basis of Quota (or positive discrimination), the people of a certain caste, gender, or ethnicity get appointed for the job while more meritorious are denied the opportunities. When a quota system under DEI is included in an institution, organisation, or nation the performance of the organisation deteriorates as there is a large number of people appointed for the job, who are not the best. As a result, when the performance of the organisation declines, it can’t compete with those organisations which do not practice the DEI. Take the example of the Indian Cricket Team, which is presently the top team in the world in all formats[3] The Indian cricket team [4](pictured above) could reach the top because there is no reservation in the cricket team, and the selection is purely based on merit. However, according to the DEI brigade, there should be a quota even in the cricket team. They claim, “In the 86 years since India attained Test status, 290 different men have played test cricket for India. However, only four belong to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. That’s four, instead of about 70, as it should have been per the population proportion. This is a disparity that just cannot be dismissed as insignificant”.[5] Imagine that a quota system is implemented in a cricket team and the players are selected on the basis of their caste or religion, instead of merit. Such a team would be perhaps the worst team in the world as the players would never work as a team and are internally divided on the basis of caste and religion. In the same way, if an organisation selects people on the basis of a Quota, like the public sector companies in India, they can never compete with the private sector companies which don’t have a Quota system. There is already a push to not only increase the Quota in India (which is already 60% plus), but also to include reservations in the private sector. A nation that implements DEI based on the quota system, can never compete with a nation which promotes merit and equality. USA has been the world leader in almost every field of life because of their merit based system. Today, India is one of the fastest-growing economies of the world and is poised to continue on this path, it is not because of the quota based public sectors, but because of merit based corporate sectors.[6] If you wish to ruin an institution, one sure way is to force quota system in the organisation to implement DEI. Hence, not only do those people hate DEI, who miss out on their opportunities, but even organisations hate the forceful implementation of DEI which reduces their performance and competitive edge in the market. If people hate DEI, it is because, PS: Some DEI supporter may question why other Indian sports is not on top, or why Indian private companies are not the best despite no reservation there, let them give the example of a sports team or company that excelled in the world due to the Quota System. The best performance can come only merit alone is valued and all people are treated equally irrespective of their caste, creed, race or gender.

Question: Why do we Indians give so much importance to government jobs?
Answer: There are many things that are determined more by tradition than by reality. Indians prefer government jobs because their parents and parent’s parent and their parents prefered government jobs. However, if you apply your mind, you'll see that the reality is quite different now. In the past, indeed government jobs were the best, much better than any private sector jobs. Let me give my own example. After my B Tech in Mechanical Engineering in 1987, from IIT (BHU) Varanasi, I got a job in L&T, which was considered to be among the most prestigious companies in India. This company used to be the dream company of almost half the students of IIT Bombay, Mechanical Engineering. I joined the company in Bangalore and worked there for one year. Do you know the salary of the Graduate Engineer Trainee (GET) then? It was only Rs 1550 + Rs 300 (HRA) per month. Back then, the starting salary of a civil servant was Rs 2500 plus government accommodation plus a phone (which used to be a very expensive and luxury item then) and a government car. To achieve the matching level of facilities and perks, you have to work for at least 15 years in L&T. In in 1980s, the Indian economy was driven by the public sector and government officials were in the driver's seat. However, the situation has changed in the last three decades. While not every student of an IIT gets a great salary, in the year 2022, 960 IIT graduates received Rs 50 lakh and above annual pay.[1] This amount is much more than the starting salary of an IAS officer, which is less than Rs 10 lakhs per annum. Even a top civil servant at the rank of cabinet secretary would not get this much of a salary. Pension was another great advantage of government services in the past. For example, a top civil servant who retired in 1990 would be getting a salary of around Rs 10,000 pm and so his pension would be around Rs 5000. However, the same civil servant, if alive today, would get a pension of more than Rs 200,000 pm today. Even after his death, his wife/spouse would get half of this amount as a pension. No private sector can match this even today. However, this Old Pension Scheme has been withdrawn since 2004 and is no longer available to government officers including IAS today. No wonder, many youngsters, who have been brought up in metro cities and educated in top colleges are not interested in government jobs today, as they have much better options available today. It is thus evident that government jobs have lost much of their sheen and are no longer the top choice for the most brilliant Indians. However, government jobs are still preferred by millions of Indians who do not have the right exposure and still take their decisions based on their parent’s wishes and value the social value of the job more than the real nature of the job. Government jobs are still important because they still provide greater job security than the private sector and you can’t be removed easily after you are appointed. Moreover, due to the high corruption in some government jobs, the officers can make so much illegal money that no employee in the private sector can even dream of. However, such jobs and such corrupt government officers are few in number and when they are caught, they end up paying huge prices for their corruption. Unfortunately, it is also not easy to work honestly in most government jobs that people aspire to, as honest officers face lots of problems including transfers, if they follow the rules and are honest. Unfortunately, the level of politicians has declined tremendously over the last few decades and it is becoming increasingly difficult to work independently in accordance with the law. In my view, if you are truly brilliant, government jobs are no longer the best option for you. Instead, you must try to get a private sector job in a top Indian or Multinational company in India or in a developed country. If you join a government job without knowing the present reality, based on the glory of the past, you may be highly disappointed and become frustrated in your future. Government jobs are good today only if you prefer job security and are not hesitant to become part of the system.

Question: What is your take on women's reservation bill which has been passed in LS in one attempt by NDA, whereas Cong failed to do so after several attempts?
Answer: Today, India is celebrating the passing of the Women's Reservation Bill, which is passed almost unanimously in both houses of Parliament. With this bill, 33% of the seats will be reserved for women in Parliament and in State Legislature. There are already 131/542 (24%) reserved seats for SC/STs in current Loksabha (84- SCs, 47- STs). It means that now almost 50% of seats of MLA/MP will be reserved in India, including women’s reservation. However, the reservation of seats is not going to stop here. There is already a demand for the reservation of seats for OBCs whose population is estimated to be between 46% to 52%.[1] Almost all the opposition parties are demanding a caste census to determine the exact population of OBCs so that they can demand reservations for them as well. If proportional number of seats are reserved for the OBCs (as done in the case of jobs), the total reservation will surpass 80%. It means that a male of an unreserved category won’t be able to contest for five out of seven seats in elections. Moreover, the seats will be rotated in every election. Hence, most current incumbent MP or MLA from general category will not be able to contest election from the same place next time, while no such bar may be there for reserved candidate, as anyone can contest from unreserved seats. As a result, the so called upper caste people, specially the males will be gradually eliminated or lose their ground gradually in India. It would be foolish to assume that the Indian politicians will be satisfied with the reservation of 33% seats in Parliament. Very soon, there will be demand for reservation of 33% seats for women in educational institutions and government jobs. We already have more than 60% reservations in central government jobs and some states have over 70% reservations in their state. If the women's reservation takes place in India, the reservation will be 80%-90% in India and only 10% to 20% of seats will be available on merit. What will happen to the performance of educational institutions and government organisations in India with such a high percentage of reservations? When India was formed after decades of freedom struggle, there was a dream of equality and justice for all. It may be worthwhile to remember the following articles of the Indian Constitution. Today, we have made a mockery of our constitution by shamelessly denying right to equality by granting reservations to people in jobs and educational institutions on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, and residence. I am against all forms of reservation because I believe that reservation is a sure recipe for mediocrity, conflict and injustice. Only when the best people are selected for education and jobs, purely on merit, the people and nation can grow to realise their full potential. The more reservation India brings into public life, the worse it will become in terms of performance, right to equality and social justice. No developed country has reserved seats in the Legislature, educational institutions and jobs as in India. We have not moved forward with the Women’s Reservation Bill, but have gone backwards by progressively increasing reservation in every domain of life and neglecting merit and performance.

Question: What governs ethical behavior? How do we decide on an ethical course of action?
Answer: Yesterday, a friend of mine who is fond of drinking forwarded the following post on our WhatsApp group. An Indian citizen Sheela donated Rs.5000 to the PM/ CM Relief Fund. On the other hand, Pandu bought a whisky bottle worth Rs 5000. The question is, who contributed more... Therefore, not only did Pandu contribute more, he created jobs at the Distillery, their suppliers of labels, bottles, caps, machinery etc., and jobs at the Marketing Company, jobs at the Wine Shop, and moreover, he was in High Spirits, doing so.! On the other side, Sheila doesn't even know where her money went...!!! Think of it...! Next time, when you Buy a Bottle of Whisky, ‘YOU’ Serve your Nation...!!! Be a Responsible Citizen. Have a lovely Monsoon and also be in High Spirits...!!! This was a post justifying not only the consumption of alcohol but even associating it with national service, much above charity. The question is does an alcoholic person contribute more to society than those who selflessly give charity to the government or the charitable organisation? In other words, which of the two (Sheela or Pandu) is more ethical? It is never easy to decide the ethicality of an action because everyone believes that what he or she is doing is a good action. Furthermore, we tend to justify our actions to avoid cognitive dissonance which is created due to conflict between our thoughts and actions. However, we can’t allow everyone to choose his own righteousness and morality of the action without taking into account the impact of the action on others, society and the nation. So how can we objectively decide which actions are moral? In my opinion, to compare the ethical value of an action, we can use the following four criteria. Let us evaluate their relative merit based on the above parameter. 1. Voluntary: The action of Sheela is voluntary, while Pandu's is involuntary since he has no option, but to pay the taxes if he wishes to consume alcohol. If there would have an option that he can buy a drink with or without paying taxes, and he would have opted to pay the taxes for the welfare of the country, we could have called it voluntary. 2. Renunciation: Sheela has sacrificed at least Rs 3500 of her money without getting any tangible benefit while Pandu made no sacrifice as he has enjoyed his drink using his money. 3. Social Good: The taxes/charity paid by both would be used by the state for social welfare. However, have you ever thought that taxes are so high (200%-300%) on certain items like Alcohol or Cigarette while other items like usually taxed at around 20% and food items are taxed at 0%? The government taxes are low for the items which are essential and good for citizens. However, items like alcohol or cigarettes (also called sometimes, SIN goods) are taxed heavily because they harm not only the consumer but also society, as most crimes like murder, rape, domestic violence, and road accidents happen under the influence of alcohol (you can get the data by Google). So some governments ban the consumption of sin goods, and if they can’t, they impose high taxes on them to reduce their consumption to minimise their negative impact on society. So, the consumption of alcohol is also not good for the individual or society. 4. Law: It appears no violation of the law is done by either person. However, if the consumption would have taken place in a prohibited state, the immorality of Pandu would have been even higher. Hence, in my opinion, the action of Sheela is much more beneficial to society and hence more ethical. When in doubt, use the four principles to determine the Ethical value of an action. The more conditions are satisfied, the more Ethical an action is. The more conditions are violated, the greater is the unethical practice.
